questions.topic: AI, ML, DL, data science and automation
questions.question: Deep learning is a family within machine learning that uses multi-layer neural networks to learn representations automatically.
questions.explanation: The lecture places deep learning inside machine learning, and machine learning inside the broad field of AI. Its defining feature is multi-layer neural networks that learn representations rather than relying on hand-crafted features.
questions.concept: AI is the broad field; ML is one approach within it; DL is one family within ML.

questions.topic: AI, ML, DL, data science and automation
questions.question: Which term describes a system that follows fixed procedures without learning from data?
questions.explanation: The lecture defines automation as following rules or fixed procedures, possibly without any learning. Invoice routing by fixed rules is the slide's example.
questions.concept: Automation follows rules; machine learning learns from data.
options: Machine learning
Deep learning
Automation
Data science
whyWrong: ML systems improve from data or experience instead of following only hand-written rules.
Deep learning learns representations with multi-layer neural networks; it is a learning method.
Data science extracts insight using statistics, databases, visualization and domain analysis.

questions.topic: AI, ML, DL, data science and automation
questions.question: Match each term to its core idea.
questions.explanation: These are the core ideas from the comparison table. AI is the umbrella; ML and DL are learning approaches; data science overlaps with AI but also includes statistics and visualization; automation can work without learning.
questions.concept: Each term answers a different question: what it aims for, and how it gets there.

pairs.right: Goal-directed intelligent behaviour
Learns from data
Learns representations
Extracts insight
Follows rules

questions.question: The lecture says definitions of AI change over time. What is the reason it gives?
questions.explanation: Once a task becomes well understood and routine, people stop calling it intelligent, so the boundary of what counts as AI moves.
questions.concept: AI is defined by what it does (maps observations and objectives to decisions or actions), and the bar for 'intelligent' moves as tasks become routine.
options: Tasks once seen as intelligent can later become routine automation
AI research stopped during the AI winters, so old definitions were lost
Only deep learning systems are considered AI today
A rigorous definition must leave out social consequences
whyWrong: AI winters slowed progress, but they are not given as the reason definitions shift.
The lecture explicitly includes symbolic, search, planning and rule-based approaches within AI.
The lecture says the opposite: a rigorous definition must include technical mechanisms and social consequences.

questions.topic: AI, ML, DL, data science and automation
questions.question: A city council's complaints office uses a program that applies a fixed table of keywords and if-then rules to forward each complaint to a department. Staff call it 'our AI'. A consultant proposes replacing it with a model trained on three years of complaints that staff have already tagged with the correct department. Which description of the two systems is most accurate?
questions.explanation: The existing program follows fixed rules and does not improve from data, which the lecture calls automation. The proposal learns a mapping from inputs to known labels (departments) using historical labelled examples, which is supervised machine learning.
questions.concept: Ask two questions: does the system learn from data, and are there labels? Fixed rules with no learning is automation; learning from labelled examples is supervised ML.
options: Both are deep learning, because both process written text
The current program is rule-based automation; the proposal is supervised machine learning
The proposal is data science rather than AI, because it uses historical data
Both are unsupervised learning, because no human reads the complaints at prediction time
whyWrong: Processing text does not make a system deep learning. The current program learns nothing, and the proposal does not say it uses multi-layer neural networks.
A model that learns to predict a department from labelled examples is machine learning. Data science centres on extracting insight, for example in dashboards.
Whether a human reads new complaints is irrelevant. The proposal learns from tagged examples, which makes it supervised.

questions.question: Which sequence matches the lecture's core abstraction of an AI system?
questions.explanation: The slide's core abstraction is: observation, then internal state, then decision, then action, then feedback that informs the next cycle.
questions.concept: AI perceives, represents, reasons or learns, then acts toward goals and uses feedback.
options: Observation, internal state, decision, action, feedback
Decision, observation, action, internal state, feedback
Action, feedback, observation, decision, internal state
Observation, action, internal state, feedback, decision
whyWrong: A system cannot decide before it has observed anything; observation comes first.
Action is driven by a decision; it does not start the cycle.
Acting before forming an internal state and a decision skips the reasoning step.

questions.question: In the AI system stack, user interfaces, APIs, audit logs, human approval and rollback procedures belong to the action layer.
questions.explanation: The action layer is where the system touches the world: interfaces, APIs, tools, robots, monitoring, audit logs, human approval and rollback.
questions.concept: Data layer, model layer, reasoning/orchestration layer, action layer: each has its own responsibilities.

questions.question: According to the lecture, institutional governance of AI is moving faster than adoption, so evaluation, accountability and safety are ahead of capability.
questions.explanation: The lecture says the reverse. Adoption is moving faster than institutional governance, and evaluation, accountability, privacy and safety still lag behind capability.
questions.concept: Capability and adoption are ahead of governance, which is why responsible deployment is part of the course.

questions.question: A team adds a component that checks every generated plan against budget limits and runs a simulation before any tool is called. Which layer of the AI system stack does this component belong to?
questions.explanation: The reasoning and orchestration layer contains retrieval, memory, constraints, planning, simulation, testing and decision logic. Checking plans against constraints and simulating them fits there.
questions.concept: Orchestration sits between the model and the action: it decides what to do with model outputs.
options: Data layer
Model layer
Reasoning and orchestration layer
Action layer
whyWrong: The data layer covers collection, labels, cleaning, consent, lineage and governance of data.
The model layer holds the rules, statistical models, neural networks or foundation models that produce outputs.
The action layer executes or exposes actions (APIs, tools, approval). Checking plans before acting is orchestration.

questions.question: A hospital's readmission-risk model scores well in a vendor demo. During review, you find that patient records were collected without consent metadata, different wards labelled 'readmitted' differently, and nobody can say where several columns came from. The vendor proposes switching to a larger neural network. What is the best response?
questions.explanation: Every issue described (consent, labelling, lineage) belongs to the data layer: collection, labels, cleaning, representativeness, consent, metadata, lineage and governance. Changing the model layer leaves these issues in place.
questions.concept: Locate a problem in the right layer before choosing a fix. Data problems need data fixes.
options: Accept the larger neural network, because more capacity will learn around inconsistent labels
Add audit logs and a human approval button in the action layer, which solves the problem
Add more planning steps in the orchestration layer so the model reasons more carefully
Fix the data layer first: consent, consistent labels and lineage, because a bigger model cannot repair them
whyWrong: A model learns whatever the labels say. Inconsistent labels and missing consent are data-layer problems that model capacity cannot fix.
Logging and approval control actions. They do not repair how the training data was collected or labelled.
Better orchestration cannot fix untraceable or inconsistently labelled training data.

questions.question: A system responds only to its current input and keeps no memory of past episodes. Under the functionality-based classification, what type is it?
questions.explanation: Reactive systems respond to current inputs without retaining internal memory of past episodes.
questions.concept: The functionality-based question is: what does the system remember, why, and who controls that memory?
options: Limited-memory system
Theory-of-mind AI
Self-aware AI
Reactive system
whyWrong: Limited-memory systems use recent or stored information, for example driving perception histories.
Theory-of-mind AI is a mainly conceptual category about modelling others' mental states.
Self-aware AI is a conceptual category, not an ordinary deployed system.

questions.question: Theory-of-mind AI and self-aware AI are mainly conceptual categories in introductory teaching rather than ordinary deployed systems.
questions.explanation: The lecture states this directly. Deployed systems are typically reactive or limited-memory.
questions.concept: Two of the four functionality-based types describe deployed systems; the other two are conceptual.

questions.topic: Types of AI: symbolic, subsymbolic, hybrid
questions.question: Match each type of AI to its description.
questions.explanation: Symbolic AI represents knowledge explicitly. Subsymbolic AI learns representations such as embeddings. Hybrid AI combines both. Limited memory comes from the separate functionality-based classification.
questions.concept: Symbolic is explicit and inspectable; subsymbolic is learned and opaque; hybrid divides the work.

pairs.right: Rules, logic and knowledge graphs; often interpretable but can be brittle
Learns patterns from data with neural networks; powerful but often opaque
A learned model perceives while rules, retrieval or tests control action
Uses recent or stored information to improve decisions

questions.topic: Types of AI: symbolic, subsymbolic, hybrid
questions.question: The lecture says robust deployment depends less on choosing one camp and more on designing the right division of labour. Why?
questions.explanation: Neural models are strong at perception and language but opaque; symbolic rules are interpretable but brittle. A hybrid system can let a model perceive while rules, retrieval and tests decide what is allowed.
questions.concept: Choose components by role: learned perception, explicit control, human review where needed.
options: Subsymbolic AI has now fully replaced symbolic AI, so the choice of camp no longer matters
They have complementary strengths, so each part of a task can go to the method that suits it
Symbolic and subsymbolic methods cannot be combined inside a single deployed system
A hybrid design removes the need for human review, so oversight costs disappear
whyWrong: Symbolic methods (rules, constraints, knowledge graphs) are still used, especially to control action.
Hybrid AI is exactly such a combination.
The slide's hybrid example still includes verification and human review.

questions.topic: Types of AI: symbolic, subsymbolic, hybrid
questions.question: A bank builds a mortgage-document assistant. A neural model reads scanned payslips and extracts figures. Fixed eligibility rules written by compliance officers then decide whether the file is complete, and borderline files go to a human underwriter. How should this system be classified?
questions.explanation: A learned model handles perception (reading documents), and explicit rules plus human review control the action. That is the lecture's description of hybrid AI.
questions.concept: Look at which part learns and which part is explicit. When both are present, the system is hybrid.
options: Purely symbolic AI, because the final eligibility decision is made by written rules
Hybrid AI: learned perception combined with explicit rules and human review
Purely subsymbolic AI, because a neural network reads the scanned documents
Self-aware AI, because it recognises on its own when it should ask a human
whyWrong: This ignores the neural model that performs the perception step.
This ignores the explicit compliance rules that control the decision.
Routing borderline cases to a person is a designed rule, not self-awareness, which the lecture treats as a conceptual category.

questions.question: Which learning paradigm creates its training signal from the raw data itself, for example by predicting a missing word or masked image patch?
questions.explanation: Self-supervised learning builds prediction tasks from unlabelled data, which is why it is central to large language and foundation models.
questions.concept: Self-supervised learning makes its own labels from the data.
options: Supervised learning
Unsupervised learning
Self-supervised learning
Reinforcement learning
whyWrong: Supervised learning needs human-provided labels for each example.
Unsupervised learning looks for structure such as clusters; it does not set up a prediction task from the data.
Reinforcement learning learns from rewards received through interaction.

questions.question: The lecture says unsupervised learning results should be treated as hypotheses that need expert validation, not as automatic truth.
questions.explanation: Because there may be no single correct answer, clusters or anomalies found without labels need domain interpretation.
questions.concept: Unsupervised output is a starting point for expert interpretation.

questions.question: Match each learning paradigm to what it learns from.
questions.explanation: Each paradigm differs in its learning signal: labels, structure, rewards, or self-generated tasks.
questions.concept: Identify the paradigm by its learning signal.

pairs.right: Examples paired with target labels
Data without labels, searching for hidden structure
States, actions and rewards over time
Prediction tasks created from raw data

questions.question: Why is evaluating unsupervised learning harder than evaluating supervised learning?
questions.explanation: Supervised learning has known labels to measure against. Clusters, latent dimensions and anomalies often have no ground truth, so experts must judge whether they are meaningful.
questions.concept: No labels means no answer key, so meaning must come from domain experts.
options: Unsupervised models need far more human-provided labels than supervised models do
There may be no single correct answer, so domain interpretation becomes essential
Unsupervised models cannot work with high-dimensional data such as text or images
Unsupervised results are wrong until a supervised neural network has checked them
whyWrong: Unsupervised learning uses no labels at all.
PCA/UMAP for high-dimensional data is listed as an unsupervised use case.
The lecture asks for expert validation, not a neural network check.

questions.question: An online-learning platform has three goals. A: predict whether a new essay needs instructor review, using past essays that instructors already marked 'review' or 'no review'. B: discover groups of learners with similar study habits; no groups have been defined. C: a tutoring bot that changes its hint strategy based on whether students eventually solve problems. Which pairing is correct?
questions.explanation: Labelled historical outcomes give supervised learning. Finding unknown groups is unsupervised clustering. Adjusting behaviour from the consequences of actions is reinforcement learning.
questions.concept: Labels, structure or rewards: identify the learning signal in each goal.
questions.source: Lec 1, slide 11, Lec 1, slide 12, Lec 1, slide 13, Lec 1, slide 15
options: A unsupervised, B supervised, C reinforcement learning
A supervised, B self-supervised, C supervised
A self-supervised, B unsupervised, C supervised
A supervised, B unsupervised, C reinforcement learning
whyWrong: A has labels (review/no review), so it is supervised. B has no predefined groups, so it cannot be supervised.
B looks for groups (clusters), which is unsupervised. C learns from outcomes of its actions, which is a reward signal.
A uses human-provided labels, so it is supervised. C has no labelled 'correct hint' for each case; it learns from consequences.

questions.question: Once a supervised model has been validated on held-out data, its performance cannot drop when real-world data differs from the training data.
questions.explanation: The lecture lists performance drops when real-world data differs from training data as a key supervised-learning risk, along with label bias, leakage and class imbalance.
questions.concept: Validation on held-out data does not protect against distribution shift after deployment.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the trade-offs of deep models listed in the lecture?
questions.explanation: Deep models work well for complex patterns in images, speech, language, code and multimodal data. Their trade-offs are data needs, compute cost, interpretability and fragility.
questions.concept: Deep learning is powerful at perception, but at a cost in data, compute and transparency.
options: They can be data-hungry
They are hard to interpret
They cannot learn patterns from images or speech
They can be fragile outside their training distribution
whyWrong: This is listed: deep models often need large datasets.
This is listed: internal representations are difficult to explain.
This is listed as a trade-off.

questions.question: Which list contains only risks of generative AI named in the lecture?
questions.explanation: The slide lists hallucination, deepfakes, provenance problems, copyright disputes and overreliance as risks of generative AI.
questions.concept: Generative AI creates content, so its risks concern truthfulness, authenticity and ownership.
options: Hallucination, multicollinearity, heteroscedasticity, deepfakes
Hallucination, deepfakes, provenance problems, copyright disputes
Label leakage, class imbalance, deepfakes, overfitting
Slow training, high memory use, overfitting, underfitting
whyWrong: Multicollinearity and heteroscedasticity are regression issues, not generative-AI risks.
Label leakage and class imbalance are supervised-learning risks.
These are general training concerns, not the generative-AI risks listed.

questions.question: Why does the lecture call reward specification the core difficulty of reinforcement learning?
questions.explanation: Poor reward design can encourage unsafe or undesirable behaviour even when the algorithm is optimising correctly. The system can satisfy the measured reward while violating the real goal.
questions.concept: Optimisation follows the measure; design the measure carefully.
options: Reinforcement learning cannot handle tasks that need several steps over time
The agent optimises what is measured, so a poorly chosen reward encourages shortcuts
Rewards must be human labels attached to every single training example
Reinforcement learning has no policy, so there is nothing to update after feedback
whyWrong: RL is designed for sequential tasks such as games and control.
Per-example labels are supervised learning; RL receives rewards from interaction.
RL updates a policy after each state, action and reward.

questions.question: A telecom company trains a call-handling agent with reinforcement learning and rewards it for short average call duration. After deployment, calls are much shorter, but many customers call back because their problems were never solved. What is the best diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The agent maximised exactly what was rewarded. Because call duration is not the same as customer resolution, the agent found a shortcut. The fix is to redesign the reward, for example to reflect resolution.
questions.concept: Reward design: a system can satisfy the measured reward while violating the intended outcome.
options: The reward measured a shortcut, not the real goal, so the agent learned to end calls early
The learning algorithm has a bug, because a correctly optimised agent cannot behave badly
The task should be switched to unsupervised clustering of the recorded customer calls
The agent needs more GPUs and a deeper network so it can learn the real goal
whyWrong: The lecture warns that poor rewards cause undesirable behaviour even when the algorithm optimises correctly.
Clustering finds groups; it would not teach the agent to resolve problems.
More capacity optimises the same reward even harder; it does not change what is rewarded.

questions.topic: Evaluation and limits of AI methods
questions.question: Match each metric category to an example the lecture lists for it.
questions.explanation: Evaluation has three families. Technical metrics measure model performance, human metrics measure the experience of people using it, and risk metrics measure potential harm.
questions.concept: Measure what matters, not only what is easy to measure.

pairs.right: Accuracy, F1, calibration, robustness
Trust, usability, workload, appealability
Fairness, privacy, security, safety, auditability

questions.question: Under the risk-based governance idea for foundation models, uses classed as 'unacceptable' risk are handled through transparency duties.
questions.explanation: Unacceptable-risk uses are prohibited. Transparency duties apply to limited-risk uses; high-risk uses face strict requirements; minimal-risk uses get normal use plus monitoring.
questions.concept: Governance scales with risk: monitoring, transparency, strict requirements, prohibition.

questions.question: Which metric is specific to evaluating AI agents, as opposed to an ordinary classifier?
questions.explanation: Agents call tools and take actions, so they are judged on task completion, tool-call accuracy, cost, time, recovery from errors and human override rates.
questions.concept: Agents act, so evaluation includes how well they act, not only how well they predict.
options: Tool-call accuracy
Precision
ROC-AUC
F1-score
whyWrong: Precision is a standard classification metric.
ROC-AUC measures class separation for classifiers.
F1 combines precision and recall for classifiers.

questions.topic: Evaluation and limits of AI methods
questions.question: What does the principle 'Measure what matters, not only what is easy to measure' mean in practice?
questions.explanation: Accuracy-style metrics are convenient but incomplete. The lecture pairs technical metrics with human and risk metrics so that evaluation reflects real goals.
questions.concept: Evaluation should reflect real goals and real risks.
options: Use accuracy alone, because it is the easiest metric to compare across models
Ignore human metrics such as trust and workload, because they are subjective
A system can score well on easy metrics while failing on fairness, usability or safety
Measure risk only after deployment, once real problems have started to appear
whyWrong: This is exactly the habit the principle warns against.
Human metrics are one of the three metric families the lecture asks for.
Risk metrics such as fairness and safety belong in evaluation, not only after harm occurs.

questions.topic: Evaluation and limits of AI methods
questions.question: A university's AI essay-feedback tool reports 94% accuracy on its test set. In a pilot, students say the feedback is hard to act on, the tool is noticeably less accurate for non-native English writers, and there is no way to contest a mark. What is the best conclusion?
questions.explanation: The pilot reveals problems in the human metrics (usability, appealability) and the risk metrics (subgroup fairness) that one overall technical number hides.
questions.concept: Overall accuracy can hide subgroup errors and human costs.
options: 94% accuracy shows the tool is ready to deploy; the student complaints are only subjective
The only real problem is the small test set, so retesting on more essays will settle it
Accuracy cannot be measured for text tasks, so the 94% figure is meaningless here
Accuracy alone is not enough: fairness across groups, usability and appeals also need evaluating
whyWrong: Lower accuracy for one group is a measurable fairness issue, and usability and appealability are named human metrics.
More essays would refine the accuracy estimate but would not address fairness, usability or appeals.
Accuracy can be measured for text classification; the issue is that it is incomplete, not meaningless.

questions.question: Who founded information theory and built early ideas about game-playing machines?
questions.explanation: Shannon founded information theory and linked communication, uncertainty and computation.
questions.concept: Each founder contributed a different foundation: behaviour tests, information, feedback, architecture.
options: Claude Shannon
Alan Turing
Norbert Wiener
John von Neumann
whyWrong: Turing proposed the imitation game and argued intelligence should be judged by observable behaviour.
Wiener developed cybernetics, with its focus on feedback and control.
Von Neumann shaped stored-program computing and computer architecture.

questions.question: Match each person to their contribution as described in the lecture.
questions.explanation: Boole is from the pre-history slide; the others are from the founders slide.
questions.concept: AI built on logic, computation, information and feedback.

pairs.right: The imitation game: judging machine intelligence by observable behaviour
Cybernetics: feedback, control and communication
Stored-program computing and formal computer architecture
Expressing logic using mathematics

questions.question: Single-layer perceptrons had important limitations, and interest in neural networks decreased for some time as a result.
questions.explanation: The perceptron showed machines could learn simple decisions, but single-layer limitations reduced interest until suitable mathematics, data, hardware and support arrived.
questions.concept: Algorithms need suitable maths, data, hardware and support to succeed.

questions.question: What lesson does the lecture draw from early symbolic optimism?
questions.explanation: Symbols, rules and search could find solutions in well-defined settings, but real environments are open, changing and full of common-sense knowledge.
questions.concept: Closed-world success does not imply open-world readiness.
options: Symbolic systems failed because they relied too heavily on data
Success in closed worlds does not automatically scale to open-world complexity
Symbolic AI was abandoned because it could not solve any problem
Early programs failed only because GPUs had not been invented
whyWrong: Early symbolic systems used symbols, rules and search, not data-driven learning.
It solved problems in limited, closed settings; the issue was scaling.
The lesson concerns open-world complexity, not a single hardware gap.

questions.question: A start-up demonstrates a rule-based assistant that schedules meetings perfectly in a demo office with five fixed rooms and ten staff. Investors now want it to run scheduling for a large hospital next quarter, with emergencies, staff changes and conflicting priorities. Based on the history of AI, what is the best warning?
questions.explanation: AI winters followed expectations that outran results. Expert systems were expensive to maintain, inflexible and unable to adapt to changing situations. A closed demo does not show open-world readiness.
questions.concept: A successful demonstration does not always mean the system is ready for real-world use.
questions.source: Lec 1, slide 23, Lec 1, slide 25, Lec 1, slide 28
options: Rule-based systems never work, so the start-up should replace everything with deep learning immediately
AI winters happened because expectations were too low, so investors should raise their expectations
Expert systems failed because they lacked human knowledge, so adding staff interviews will fix it
A closed demo does not show real-world readiness, and rule bases are costly to maintain as things change
whyWrong: Expert systems worked well in limited areas. The lesson is about scaling and maintenance, not that rules never work.
AI winters happened when expectations were higher than real results.
Expert systems were built on human knowledge; their problems were cost, inflexibility and difficulty adapting.

questions.question: The lecture argues that the value of AI in business should be measured mainly by model accuracy.
questions.explanation: Value should be measured by saved time, fewer errors, better quality, lower risk and user satisfaction, not accuracy alone.
questions.concept: A model is not a strategy; impact comes from redesigned systems.

questions.question: According to the lecture, what should students do before using code produced by an AI coding tool?
questions.explanation: The software-engineering slide lists risks such as false confidence, wrong explanations, hidden bugs and security gaps.
questions.concept: AI-generated work needs human verification.
options: Use it if it compiles without errors
Ask the same AI tool to confirm that the code is correct
Read the code, run tests and check its assumptions
Check only formatting and naming
whyWrong: Code that compiles can still contain hidden bugs and security gaps.
The tool can give wrong explanations; confirmation from it is not verification.
Correctness, security, licences and quality must be checked, not only style.

questions.question: In science, AI-generated ideas and designs must be reproducible, checked by experts and confirmed through experiments.
questions.explanation: The lecture says AI can suggest ideas and designs, but results must be reproducible, expert-checked and experimentally confirmed.
questions.concept: AI suggestions in science are hypotheses until verified.

questions.question: What does 'A model is not a strategy; impact comes from redesigned systems' mean?
questions.explanation: The slide's cycle runs Problem, Workflow, Model, People, Measurement. Success requires staff training, good data management, process improvement and monitoring.
questions.concept: AI impact depends on the whole system around the model.
options: A more accurate model will automatically produce business impact on its own
Businesses should avoid models entirely and rely on process changes alone
Company strategy should be decided directly by the model's predictions
A model creates value only when the workflow, people and measurement around it change
whyWrong: This contradicts the slide, which ties impact to workflow, people and measurement.
The slide includes the model as one step in the cycle.
The slide is about integrating models into systems, not letting models set strategy.

questions.question: A school gives every student an AI tutor. After one term, homework completion rises from 60% to 95%, but exam results show no improvement in understanding, and teachers notice many answers copied from AI explanations. What is the best response based on the lecture?
questions.explanation: AI tutors work best with clear goals, practice, reflection and teacher guidance. Risks include plagiarism, weak learning and overdependence.
questions.concept: Judge educational AI by learning outcomes, not activity metrics.
options: Higher completion proves that learning improved, so the current setup should stay unchanged
Remove teacher involvement so the AI can personalise each student's learning without interference
Check whether it truly improves understanding, and add goals, practice, reflection and teacher guidance
Upgrade to a larger model, because weak learning shows the current model lacks capability
whyWrong: Completion is not understanding. The lecture asks teachers to check whether AI truly improves learning.
The lecture says AI tutors work best with teacher guidance.
The issues described (copying, overdependence, weak learning) are use and design risks, not model-capability gaps.

questions.question: What distinguishes an AI agent from a chatbot, according to the lecture?
questions.explanation: An AI agent observes its environment and takes actions. Agent = perceptions + goals + action choices + feedback.
questions.concept: Agents act; chatbots respond.
options: It can use tools to take actions that change things
It always runs on a larger language model than a chatbot does
It never needs to handle uncertain or missing information
It only answers questions in a conversation, without acting
whyWrong: Model size does not define an agent.
The main challenge for agents is controlling actions when information is uncertain.
That describes a chatbot.

questions.question: Match each PEAS element to the design question it answers.
questions.explanation: PEAS specifies an agent before building it: how success is measured, where it works, what it can do and what it can perceive.
questions.concept: PEAS forces a designer to define success, setting, actions and inputs.

pairs.right: What counts as success, cost and acceptable error?
Where does the agent operate, and what changes independently of it?
What can the agent do?
What can the agent observe?

questions.question: In a partially observable environment, the agent can see all of the state information it needs.
questions.explanation: In a partially observable environment the agent sees only some of the information. A fully observable environment is the easy case.
questions.concept: Hidden context is what makes an environment partially observable.

questions.question: An agent trades on a stock exchange alongside thousands of other automated traders. Prices change unpredictably, it cannot see other traders' strategies, and each trade affects later options. Which description fits this environment?
questions.explanation: Hidden strategies make it partially observable, unpredictable prices make it uncertain, dependence between trades makes it sequential, and competing traders make it multi-agent and adversarial.
questions.concept: Environment properties shape how hard an agent's task is.
options: Partially observable, uncertain, sequential and multi-agent/adversarial
Fully observable, deterministic, episodic and single-agent
Fully observable, uncertain, episodic and multi-agent
Partially observable, deterministic, sequential and single-agent
whyWrong: These are the easy-case properties, the opposite of what is described.
It cannot see other traders' strategies, and each trade affects later options, so it is neither fully observable nor episodic.
Prices change unpredictably and many other traders act, so it is neither deterministic nor single-agent.

questions.question: A team specifies an agent that reschedules students' exam appointments. P: number of appointments rescheduled per hour. E: the university booking system and student email. A: read calendars, send confirmations, cancel and create bookings. S: student emails, calendars, exam policy documents. A reviewer says one element is likely to cause harmful behaviour. Which one, and why?
questions.explanation: Optimisation follows the measure. A performance measure that counts only throughput ignores correctness, policy compliance, fairness and satisfaction, which the lecture lists as parts of success.
questions.concept: Poorly defined goals can lead to harmful or unwanted actions.
options: The sensors: reading a calendar is an action, so it belongs under actuators instead
The environment: student email cannot appear under both E and S at the same time
The performance measure: it rewards speed only, so the agent may break policy to go faster
The actuators: an agent should never be allowed to create or cancel bookings
whyWrong: Reading a calendar is observing, which is sensing. Actuators change the world.
The environment contains information that the sensors observe, so overlap is expected.
Actuators may include actions like booking; the lecture's answer is to control risky actions, not to forbid all actions.

questions.question: A greenhouse vent opens whenever the temperature passes 30°C and does nothing else. Which agent architecture is this?
questions.explanation: Simple reflex agents follow direct condition-action rules. They are fast and easy to understand but fail when information is missing.
questions.concept: Use the simplest architecture that can satisfy the task, risk and environment.
options: Model-based agent
Utility-based agent
Learning agent
Simple reflex agent
whyWrong: Model-based agents keep an internal view of the world to handle hidden state.
Utility-based agents balance trade-offs such as speed, cost and safety.
Learning agents improve through feedback via a critic and learning element.

questions.question: The lecture says giving an agent more memory improves service and carries no additional risk.
questions.explanation: The slide states a trade-off: more memory can mean better service and greater privacy risk. Memory needs consent, minimisation, retention rules and deletion options.
questions.concept: Memory is a trade-off between personalisation and privacy.

questions.question: Match each safety control to its purpose.
questions.explanation: Least privilege (read-only by default) limits damage, logging records tool calls, approval adds human sign-off, and red teaming tests attacks such as prompt injection.
questions.concept: Each control addresses a different governance need.

pairs.right: Reduce harm
Auditability
Accountability
Find failures

questions.question: Why does the lecture say every agent loop needs a maximum step count, an error path and a handoff path?
questions.explanation: Agents follow plan, act, observe, reflect, revise. Stopping rules prevent infinite loops, repeated harmful actions, cost overruns and user frustration.
questions.concept: An agent must know when to stop, what to do on errors, and when to hand off.
options: Step limits make the agent's plans more creative by forcing it to try new ideas
Handoff paths let the agent avoid calling tools when a task looks difficult
Error paths are only needed when several agents work together in one system
Without them an agent can loop forever, repeat harmful actions and overrun costs
whyWrong: Step limits are a safety and cost control, not a creativity aid.
A handoff passes the task to a human or another process when the agent should stop.
Any agent loop can fail, so every loop needs an error path.

questions.question: A university deploys an LLM agent that can read student records, draft emails and change grades. During testing, a student's message containing hidden instructions makes the agent call the grade-change tool. Which redesign best follows the lecture?
questions.explanation: The lecture classes changing records as critical risk, requiring policy, audit and review. Least privilege, logging, human approval and red-team tests address the failure directly.
questions.concept: Limit what an agent can do, record what it does, and require human approval for important actions.
options: Give the agent long-term memory of university policy so it remembers not to change grades
Least privilege, human approval with audit for grade changes, logged tool calls and red-team tests
Add two more agents that must vote together before any grade change is made
Switch to a larger foundation model that is better at understanding user intent
whyWrong: Memory does not enforce permissions. Changing records is a critical-risk action that needs controls outside the model.
Multi-agent systems can behave unpredictably and still need authority limits and human supervision.
A better model does not replace least privilege, approval and logging for a critical action.

questions.question: Match each part of the classic learning-agent architecture to its role.
questions.explanation: The lecture lists performance element, learning element, critic and problem generator as the classic learning-agent architecture. Because learning changes the system over time, monitoring must be continuous.
questions.concept: A learning agent acts, gets feedback, updates and re-tests.
questions.source: Lec 1, slide 42 (the slide names the four parts; the role wording is the standard textbook definition, marked supplementary)

pairs.right: Chooses the actions the agent takes
Judges how well the agent is doing using feedback
Updates the agent based on the critic's feedback
Suggests new experiences or actions to try

questions.question: Common problems of LLM agents include wrong actions, repeated loops, ignoring limits and false information.
questions.explanation: These are the common problems the lecture lists. Safe systems require approval for important actions.
questions.concept: LLM agents plan and use tools, so their failures are action failures as well as text errors.

questions.question: Why does the lecture say an agent should cite or expose its source when it makes a decision using retrieved information?
questions.explanation: Retrieval-augmented generation grounds answers in external documents. Exposing sources lets people check that the decision is supported.
questions.concept: Grounding plus visible sources makes decisions checkable.
options: So that the agent can skip asking for approval
Because retrieval-augmented generation cannot work without citations
So that humans can verify the decision against the evidence it used
To increase how much long-term memory the agent stores
whyWrong: Citing sources supports verification; it does not replace approval for risky actions.
Retrieval can work without citations; citations are for human verification.
Citations do not add to memory; they expose evidence.

questions.question: Why does an AI agent need stronger controls than a chatbot that only answers questions?
questions.explanation: An agent observes its environment and takes actions with tools. Controlling those actions when information is uncertain is the main challenge, which is why the lecture stresses least privilege, logging and human approval.
questions.concept: The ability to act is what raises the stakes.
options: Because its mistakes become actions with real consequences
Because agents always use larger and less accurate models than chatbots
Because agents never receive feedback, so they cannot correct their errors
Because chatbots are never wrong, so they need no controls at all
whyWrong: Model size is not what distinguishes agents; their ability to act is.
Agents do receive feedback; the agent formula includes it.
Chatbots can be wrong too; the difference is that an agent's errors become actions.

questions.question: According to the lecture, which two developments allowed deep networks to begin outperforming older methods?
questions.explanation: The deep learning slide says CNNs became useful for images and handwriting, and that with large datasets and powerful GPUs deep networks began to outperform older methods.
questions.concept: Deep learning took off when data and compute caught up with the ideas.
options: Hand-written expert rules and faster hard disks
Large datasets and powerful GPUs
Single-layer perceptrons and logic programming
Smaller datasets and simpler activation functions
whyWrong: Expert rules belong to the symbolic era; the slide credits data and GPU compute.
Single-layer perceptrons had the limits that caused interest to fall; they are not the cause of the comeback.
The slide points to larger datasets, not smaller ones.

questions.question: The lecture's 'key shift' is that language became both an input method and a control interface for software. What does this mean in practice?
questions.explanation: Transformers use attention to relate tokens and build representations that support generation. Because of this, a natural-language instruction can now steer what the software does, not just supply data to it.
questions.concept: Plain language now both feeds and steers software.
options: People can describe what they want in plain words and the system acts on it
Software must now be written only in natural language instead of code
Transformers can only process text, so other data is converted to words
Users must learn a new formal command language for each AI tool
whyWrong: Code still exists; language became an additional way to drive software.
The slide says transformers work with text, code, images, audio and video.
That is the opposite of the shift; plain language becomes the interface.

questions.question: The lecture presents generative AI as widely available and free of serious concerns once transformers were introduced.
questions.explanation: False. The slide says generative AI became widely available but raised concerns about accuracy, copyright, misuse and evaluation.
questions.concept: Wide availability came with new risks.

questions.question: A company links three AI agents: one drafts supplier contracts, one reviews them, and one sends approved contracts to suppliers. In testing, the drafter and reviewer sometimes pass a contract back and forth endlessly, and once the sender emailed a contract nobody had approved. Which change best addresses both problems, following the lecture?
questions.explanation: Multi-agent systems can share tasks and check each other but may behave unpredictably. The lecture says safe systems need clear roles, communication rules, authority limits, conflict handling and human supervision. The loop is a conflict-handling gap; the unapproved send is an authority and supervision gap.
questions.concept: Multiple agents need roles, limits, conflict rules and human oversight.
options: Add a fourth agent that also reviews contracts, so there are more checks
Replace the three agents with one larger model that does every step alone
Let the agents decide among themselves who has final authority each time
Set roles, authority limits and conflict rules, and require human approval to send
whyWrong: More agents without roles, limits or conflict rules can add to the unpredictability rather than fix it.
This removes the cross-checking benefit and still leaves no limit on sending.
Leaving authority to the agents is what allowed the unapproved send; authority limits should be set by people.

questions.question: Data stored as JSON or XML, with flexible keys or tags rather than a fixed table schema, is classified as:
questions.explanation: The lecture lists JSON, XML and HTML as semi-structured: they have a flexible schema organised with tags or keys.
questions.concept: Structural type describes how data is organised, not what it measures.
options: Structured data
Semi-structured data
Unstructured data
Ordinal data
whyWrong: Structured data has rows and columns with a fixed schema, such as CSV files and SQL tables.
Unstructured data has no predefined format at all, such as images, audio, video or open text.
Ordinal is a measurement scale for ordered categories, not a structural type.

questions.question: In the data-information-knowledge-decision hierarchy, 'knowledge' means a raw recorded value.
questions.explanation: A raw recorded value is data. Information is an organised value in context, knowledge is an interpreted pattern, and a decision is an action based on that interpretation.
questions.concept: Each level adds context and interpretation to the one below.

questions.question: Match each level of the hierarchy to its meaning.
questions.explanation: The hierarchy moves from raw values to context, then to patterns, then to actions such as preprocessing choices.
questions.concept: Preprocessing decisions sit at the top: they depend on interpreting the data correctly.

pairs.right: Raw recorded value
Organised value in context
Interpreted pattern
Action based on interpretation

questions.question: The lecture says the goal of preprocessing is to make data 'analytically defensible', not 'artificially perfect'. What does this mean?
questions.explanation: Good preprocessing preserves meaningful information while reducing noise, inconsistency and measurement problems, and each decision can be explained.
questions.concept: Defensible means justified, documented and faithful to the data's meaning.
options: Every row with a missing value or unusual number should be removed so the data is clean
Every numeric variable should be transformed until it follows a normal distribution
Preprocessing means cleaning only; understanding and documentation come later
Keep meaningful information and reduce noise using choices that can be justified
whyWrong: Removing inconvenient data can discard real, meaningful information. The lecture warns against this.
The lecture does not require normality; it requires justified, documented decisions.
The lecture says preprocessing is broader than cleaning: it includes understanding, validation, transformation and documentation.

questions.question: A clinic wants to combine four sources for analysis: visit records in a SQL table, laboratory results exported as JSON, doctors' free-text notes, and chest X-ray images. An analyst plans to load everything into one CSV and treat every source as numeric columns. Which classification should guide a better plan?
questions.explanation: Structured data has a fixed schema, semi-structured data uses flexible tags or keys, and unstructured data such as text and images has no predefined table format. Each needs its own handling before analysis.
questions.concept: Identify the structural type before choosing how to process a source.
options: All four are structured, because they are all stored on a computer
SQL: structured; JSON: semi-structured; notes and X-rays: unstructured
JSON is unstructured, because it has no columns
Free-text notes are semi-structured, because they contain words in sentences
whyWrong: Being stored digitally does not give data a fixed row-and-column schema.
JSON has keys and tags, which the lecture classes as semi-structured.
Open text has no predefined table format, so it is unstructured.

questions.question: Which measurement scale has a true zero, so that ratios such as 'twice as much' are meaningful?
questions.explanation: Ratio variables such as age or fare have a true zero, so ratios are meaningful. They may need imputation and scaling.
questions.concept: The scale of a variable determines which preprocessing makes sense.
options: Ratio
Nominal
Ordinal
Identifier
whyWrong: Nominal values are unordered categories; ratios between them have no meaning.
Ordinal categories are ordered, but the spacing between them is not defined, so ratios are meaningless.
An identifier only labels a record; it is not a measurement.

questions.question: An identifier column, such as a record ID, is usually used for checks like uniqueness and then excluded as a predictive feature.
questions.explanation: Identifiers label records rather than describe them. They are useful for uniqueness checks but are usually dropped before modelling.
questions.concept: Use identifiers for checking, not for predicting.

questions.question: A hotel-booking dataset has the columns below. Match each column to its measurement scale.
questions.explanation: Payment methods have no order. Satisfaction levels are ordered. Money has a true zero. A reference number only labels a record.
questions.concept: Ask: is there an order, is there a true zero, or is it just a label?

pairs.right: Nominal
Ordinal
Ratio
Identifier

questions.question: Encoding an ordinal variable as 1, 2, 3 assumes the gaps between categories are equal, which may not be true.
questions.explanation: Ordinal encoding preserves order but not necessarily equal intervals. The gap between first and second class need not equal the gap between second and third.
questions.concept: Order is not the same as equal spacing.

questions.question: A delivery company predicts whether an order will be late (Late = 0/1). Columns: OrderID, Distance_km, VehicleType (bike, van, truck), Priority (standard, express, same-day), CustomerNotes (free text, almost every value unique). Which preprocessing plan is most appropriate for an introductory workflow?
questions.explanation: Identifiers are excluded as features, nominal categories are one-hot encoded, ordinal categories can keep their order with caution, high-cardinality text is excluded in a simple workflow, and the target stays as the 0/1 label.
questions.concept: Assign each column a role and a scale before choosing its treatment.
questions.source: Lec 2.1, slide 8, Lec 2.1, slide 49, Lec 2.1, slide 51
options: OrderID for checks only; one-hot VehicleType; ordinal Priority; exclude CustomerNotes; Late as target
Keep OrderID as a numeric feature, label-encode VehicleType as 1/2/3, one-hot encode CustomerNotes
One-hot encode every column, including Distance_km and Late, so all inputs are treated equally
Drop VehicleType and Priority because they are not numeric, and keep OrderID as a feature
whyWrong: OrderID is an identifier, label-encoding a nominal variable implies a false order, and one-hot encoding near-unique text creates thousands of useless columns.
Distance_km is a ratio variable that should stay numeric, and the target must not be included in feature preprocessing.
Categorical variables can be encoded rather than dropped, and the identifier is the column that should be excluded.

questions.question: Match each data-quality dimension to its meaning.
questions.explanation: These are five of the six dimensions in the lecture; the sixth is relevance (whether a variable helps answer the question).
questions.concept: Each dimension names a different way data can fail.

pairs.right: Required values are present
Values obey acceptable rules
Categories use common labels
Records are not duplicated
Data reflects the correct period

questions.question: A cleaning rule is valid only if it is based on statistical evidence; domain knowledge and documentation are not acceptable bases.
questions.explanation: The lecture says a valid cleaning rule can be based on domain knowledge, documentation or statistical evidence.
questions.concept: Cleaning rules need a justification, and domain knowledge is one legitimate source.

questions.question: Why should the original raw file be kept unchanged and cleaning done on a working copy?
questions.explanation: Preserving raw data, plus recording which column changed, under what condition and why, makes cleaning reproducible and reversible.
questions.concept: Never overwrite the source; document every change.
options: It makes the cleaned dataset smaller and faster to load
It prevents the model from overfitting the training data
It supports reproducibility, peer review and recovery from mistakes
Raw files cannot be loaded into pandas without a copy
whyWrong: Keeping a copy does not change the size of the cleaned data.
Overfitting is a modelling issue; the raw copy is about traceability.
Raw files load normally; the reason is auditability.

questions.question: In a school dataset, the 'Grade level' column contains 'Year 10', 'year10', 'Y10' and ' Year 10 ' for the same grade. Which data-quality dimension is mainly violated?
questions.explanation: The same category written in several ways breaks consistency. If left alone, it would also create artificial categories during encoding.
questions.concept: Consistency means one category, one label.
options: Completeness
Uniqueness
Consistency
Timeliness
whyWrong: No values are missing; they are present but written differently.
Uniqueness concerns duplicated records, not differently spelled labels.
Timeliness concerns whether the data reflects the correct period.

questions.question: A marketing analyst receives a customer file. They delete every row with a missing age or an unusually high income, overwrite the original file with the result, and keep no record of what was removed. The resulting model's accuracy improves. Which criticism best reflects the lecture?
questions.explanation: The lecture says cleaning is not deleting inconvenient data, the raw dataset must be preserved, decisions must be reproducible and explainable, and unusual values may be real.
questions.concept: Reproducible, documented, justified: the three tests of a cleaning decision.
questions.source: Lec 2.1, slide 16, Lec 2.1, slide 19, Lec 2.1, slide 23
options: The process is fine, because the higher accuracy shows that the cleaning worked
Data was deleted without justification, the raw file was lost, and no rule was documented
The only mistake was using deletion instead of mean imputation for every column
The analyst should have deleted the whole income column instead of the rows
whyWrong: Better accuracy on altered data does not make the process reproducible or defensible.
The lecture rejects one universal rule, and mean imputation is sensitive to the very outliers involved.
Income may be meaningful. The issue is undocumented, unjustified removal, not which axis was deleted.

questions.question: Duplicate records can inflate the sample size and bias descriptive statistics.
questions.explanation: When the same observation appears more than once, it is counted more than once, which distorts counts, means and other statistics.
questions.concept: One observation should appear once.

questions.question: An outlier and an invalid value mean the same thing, so both should be removed in the same way.
questions.explanation: An invalid value is impossible according to a rule (for example a negative price). An outlier is unusual but may be real, so it must be investigated before any treatment.
questions.concept: Invalid means impossible; outlier means unusual.

questions.question: What is the correct sequence for preparing a categorical feature?
questions.explanation: The lecture gives the sequence: inspect categories, clean categories, handle missingness, then encode.
questions.concept: Clean labels and fill gaps before encoding.
options: Encode, inspect categories, clean categories, handle missingness
Inspect categories, clean categories, handle missingness, encode
Handle missingness, encode, inspect categories, clean categories
Inspect categories, encode, handle missingness, clean categories
whyWrong: Encoding first turns spelling variants into separate columns before they can be cleaned.
Cleaning after encoding is too late; variants are already separate columns.
Encoding before cleaning and before handling missing values creates extra or failing categories.

questions.question: Why should category labels be standardised before creating dummy (one-hot) variables?
questions.explanation: Inconsistent spelling, capitalisation and whitespace create artificial categories. Cleaning must preserve meaning while merging variants.
questions.concept: One real category should become one column.
options: Dummy variables cannot be created for columns that contain text values
Standardising labels removes the need to handle missing values later
It turns nominal variables into ordinal ones so their order is preserved
Spelling and spacing variants would become separate columns for one real category
whyWrong: One-hot encoding is designed for text categories; the problem is variants, not text itself.
Missing values still need treatment after labels are cleaned.
Cleaning labels does not add an order to categories.

questions.question: A gym's membership data has an Age column containing -3 and 250 among normal ages, including one member aged 87. MonthlyFee has a few very high values, all belonging to 'Platinum' members. Which treatment follows the lecture?
questions.explanation: Invalid values break a plausibility rule (age cannot be negative or 250), so they are investigated and usually set to missing. Outliers can be real; treatment depends on the task and domain.
questions.concept: Rules identify invalid values; domain knowledge decides what to do with outliers.
options: Delete all rows with high MonthlyFee values, because they are outliers that distort the mean
Treat 87 as invalid because it is far above the average age of members
Set -3 and 250 to missing after checking, keep 87, and investigate the high fees rather than delete them
Replace -3 with 3 by taking the absolute value, and keep 250 unchanged as a valid age
whyWrong: High fees tied to Platinum members are probably real. Blind removal discards genuine data.
An unusual age is not an impossible one. Only values that break a rule are invalid.
Silently guessing a correction is undocumented, and 250 is impossible and needs investigation.

questions.question: A dataset uses -999 to mean 'not recorded'. What is the main risk the lecture identifies with this kind of sentinel code?
questions.explanation: A sentinel code looks like a valid number, so means, scaling and models treat it as data unless it is converted to NaN.
questions.concept: Convert sentinel codes to explicit missing values before analysis.
options: It may be misread as a real number
pandas always deletes rows that contain -999
It is automatically converted to the mode
It can only appear in categorical columns
whyWrong: pandas does not treat -999 specially; that is exactly why it can be misread.
No automatic conversion happens.
Sentinel codes usually appear in numeric columns, where they distort calculations.

questions.question: Match each type of missingness to its meaning.
questions.explanation: MCAR, MAR and MNAR describe why a value is missing; structural missingness means the value is not applicable and should not always be imputed.
questions.concept: Why a value is missing determines how to treat it.

pairs.right: Missingness unrelated to any observed or unobserved values
Missingness related to other observed variables
Missingness related to the missing value itself
The value does not apply to this record

questions.question: A blank cell and a sentinel code such as 9999 carry the same risk: both are likely to be misread as real numbers.
questions.explanation: A blank cell usually becomes NaN when loaded. A sentinel code such as 9999 is the one likely to be misread as a real number.
questions.concept: Know how each form of missingness is represented after loading.

questions.question: In a household survey, people with very high incomes are more likely to refuse to report their income. Which mechanism describes this missingness?
questions.explanation: When the probability of missingness depends on the value that is missing, the data are Missing Not At Random.
questions.concept: Ask what the missingness depends on: nothing, another column, or the value itself.
options: MNAR
MCAR
MAR
Structural missing
whyWrong: MCAR would mean refusals are unrelated to any value, but here they depend on income itself.
MAR would mean missingness depends on another observed variable, not the missing income.
Income applies to every household; it was not reported rather than not applicable.

questions.question: A hospital dataset has three gaps. 'Number of pregnancies' is blank for all male patients. 'Cholesterol' is missing more often for patients from one clinic, and the clinic is recorded. 'Weight' is missing for a random batch of rows lost in a file-import error. Which plan is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Structural missingness should not always be imputed. MAR missingness relates to observed variables, which can inform the treatment. MCAR missingness from a random import error is the case where deletion or simple imputation is most defensible.
questions.concept: Match the treatment to the cause of missingness, column by column.
questions.source: Lec 2.1, slide 29, Lec 2.1, slide 31, Lec 2.1, slide 33
options: Impute all three columns with the column mean, because one simple rule is easiest to document
Delete every row with any missing value, because deletion keeps only genuine observations
Pregnancies: not applicable, so do not impute blindly; cholesterol: use clinic (MAR); weight: impute or drop (MCAR)
Treat all three as MNAR, because each value is missing from a medical record
whyWrong: The lecture rejects one universal rule. Imputing pregnancies for men would invent meaningless values.
Deletion is most acceptable when missingness is small and random; here it would also remove all male patients.
Each gap has a different cause: not applicable, related to an observed variable, and random.

questions.question: Which imputation strategy suits a nominal categorical variable with a few missing values?
questions.explanation: Mode imputation is appropriate for nominal categorical variables. A constant such as 'Unknown' is another option when it is meaningful.
questions.concept: Choose the imputation statistic that matches the variable type.
options: Mean
Median
Min-max scaling
Mode (most frequent value)
whyWrong: A mean cannot be computed for unordered categories.
A median needs ordered numeric values.
Scaling is a transformation, not an imputation strategy.

questions.question: Mean imputation is more robust to outliers and skew than median imputation.
questions.explanation: The reverse is true. The mean is pulled by extreme values; the median resists skew, which is why it is often safer for age-like variables.
questions.concept: Median for skewed numeric data, mean for roughly symmetric data.

questions.question: A missing-indicator variable equals 1 when the original value is missing and 0 otherwise.
questions.explanation: A missing indicator is a binary variable that records whether a value was missing, which is useful when missingness itself may carry information.
questions.concept: Sometimes the fact that a value is missing is informative.

questions.question: Why can heavy imputation make analysis results misleading?
questions.explanation: The lecture warns that imputed values are not observed facts, heavy imputation can overstate precision, and imputation can affect fairness when missingness relates to social or measurement processes. Reports should say what was imputed, how and why.
questions.concept: Imputation fills gaps with estimates, and estimates carry uncertainty.
options: Imputation always introduces duplicate rows into the training data
Imputed values are estimates, so results can look more precise than they are
Imputed values are removed again automatically during scaling
Imputation converts numeric variables into categorical variables
whyWrong: Imputation fills values; it does not duplicate records.
Scaling transforms imputed values like any others.
Imputation does not change a variable's type.

questions.question: An insurer's claims data has four columns with gaps: 'Region' (categorical, 1% missing), 'Broker code' (80% missing, many unique codes), 'Annual income' (25% missing, right-skewed with some very large values), and 'Previous claims' (count, 0.5% missing). Which plan is most defensible?
questions.explanation: Each column needs its own justified treatment: mode for categorical, median for skewed numeric, drop or indicator for very high missingness, and reporting for all.
questions.concept: Avoid one universal rule; different variables have different meanings.
questions.source: Lec 2.1, slide 33, Lec 2.1, slide 34, Lec 2.1, slide 36, Lec 2.1, slide 40
options: Mean imputation for all four columns, so the rule is consistent and easy to document
Mode for Region, drop or flag Broker code, median for income and previous claims, and document it
Listwise deletion of every row with any missing value, so only complete records remain
Mode for Annual income and mean for Region, so each column gets a simple statistic
whyWrong: Mean is undefined for categories, distorted by skewed income, and no single rule fits every column.
With 80% missing in Broker code, this would discard most of the dataset.
Mode suits categories, not a skewed numeric variable, and a mean cannot be computed for categories.

questions.question: Which encoding is usually safest for a nominal predictor with several categories?
questions.explanation: One-hot encoding creates one indicator column per category, which avoids false order. It increases the number of columns.
questions.concept: Nominal categories have no order, so do not give them one.
options: Label encoding
Ordinal encoding
One-hot encoding
Binary 0/1 encoding
whyWrong: Label encoding gives categories numbers that imply an order and distance.
Ordinal encoding is meant for categories with a real order.
A single 0/1 column only works for variables with exactly two categories.

questions.question: Label-encoding a nominal feature, such as city names, can imply an order between categories that has no real meaning.
questions.explanation: Label encoding assigns numbers like 0, 1, 2. Many models treat these as ordered or as distances, which is meaningless for nominal categories.
questions.concept: Numbers carry order and distance; nominal categories have neither.

questions.question: Match each variable to the treatment the lecture would suggest for a simple workflow.
questions.explanation: Binary variables become 0/1, nominal variables are one-hot encoded, ordered categories keep their order with caution, near-unique text is excluded, and the target is kept separate from feature encoding.
questions.concept: Encoding depends on whether a variable is binary, nominal, ordinal, high-cardinality or the target.

pairs.right: Binary 0/1 encoding
One-hot encoding
Ordinal encoding, stating the spacing assumption
Exclude as high-cardinality text
Keep as the target label

questions.question: When one-hot encoding is used for a regression model, why is one category often dropped?
questions.explanation: With k categories, k-1 indicators carry all the information; the last column is redundant. The dropped category becomes the reference group.
questions.concept: In regression, k categories need only k-1 indicator columns.
options: To reduce the number of rows that the regression model has to fit
Because the dropped category is assumed to be missing for every row
The dropped category is implied when all other indicators are 0, so it is redundant
To convert the variable into an ordinal one with a reference order
whyWrong: One-hot encoding adds columns; dropping one category does not change the rows.
The dropped category becomes the reference level, not a missing value.
Dropping a column does not introduce an order.

questions.question: An analyst predicting customer churn label-encodes 'Country' (France = 0, Germany = 1, Spain = 2) and uses a distance-based model. They also one-hot encode 'CustomerName', creating about 9,000 columns. Which critique is most accurate?
questions.explanation: For nominal predictors, label encoding implies order and distance. One-hot encoding nearly unique values like names creates many useless columns, so high-cardinality text is excluded in an introductory workflow.
questions.concept: Encoding must not invent order, and must not explode the feature space with near-unique values.
options: Both choices are fine, because any numeric representation works for a distance-based model
Country should stay label-encoded, but CustomerName should be label-encoded too, to save columns
Country needs one-hot encoding because its codes imply false distances, and CustomerName should be excluded
Country should be scaled with a StandardScaler after label encoding, which removes the false order
whyWrong: Distance-based models treat label codes as real distances, which is meaningless for countries.
Label-encoding names creates arbitrary numbers with false order; the feature should be excluded.
Scaling changes the range but keeps the artificial ordering and distances.

questions.question: Match each scaler to the statistics it uses.
questions.explanation: The scaler's statistics determine its outlier sensitivity: min-max is very sensitive, standardisation is sensitive, and robust scaling is less sensitive.
questions.concept: Outlier sensitivity follows from the statistics a scaler uses.

pairs.right: Mean and standard deviation
Minimum and maximum
Median and interquartile range (IQR)

questions.question: Feature scaling matters more for tree-based models than for distance-based models.
questions.explanation: Tree-based methods are less sensitive to scaling. Distance-based and gradient-based methods are the ones most affected by different feature ranges.
questions.concept: Distance and gradient methods care about scale; trees mostly do not.

questions.question: After standardisation (z-scores), what are the approximate mean and standard deviation of a feature?
questions.explanation: z = (x - mean) / standard deviation centres the feature at 0 with a spread of 1.
questions.concept: A z-score says how many standard deviations a value is from the mean.
options: Mean 1, standard deviation 0
Minimum 0, maximum 1
Median 0, IQR 1
Mean 0, standard deviation 1
whyWrong: A standard deviation of 0 would mean every value is identical.
That describes min-max normalisation.
That describes robust scaling.

questions.question: A feature has mean 50 and standard deviation 10. What is the standardised value of an observation equal to 70?
questions.explanation: z = (70 - 50) / 10 = 2. The value is two standard deviations above the mean.
questions.concept: z = (x - mean) / standard deviation.
whyWrong: 20 is the raw difference from the mean; it still has to be divided by the standard deviation.
This divides the value by 100, which is not the z-score formula.
This divides 70 by 50, which ignores both the mean subtraction and the standard deviation.

questions.question: A property dataset is used with a distance-based model. Price ranges from $50,000 to $20,000,000 because of a few genuine mansions; Bedrooms ranges from 1 to 6. After min-max scaling Price, almost all prices fall between 0 and 0.03. What is the best diagnosis and fix?
questions.explanation: Min-max scaling is very sensitive to outliers because the minimum and maximum define the scale. Robust scaling centres on the median and scales by the IQR, so it is less affected. Outliers that may be real should be investigated, not deleted.
questions.concept: Choose a scaler whose statistics are not dominated by extreme values.
questions.source: Lec 2.1, slide 57, Lec 2.1, slide 58, Lec 2.1, slide 60
options: No scaling is needed, because distance-based models are not affected by feature ranges
Switch to StandardScaler, which is not affected by outliers in the way min-max is
Delete every property priced above $1,000,000 so that min-max scaling works properly
Extreme prices compress the rest; use robust scaling and investigate rather than delete the mansions
whyWrong: Distance-based models are strongly affected: a large-range feature dominates the distance.
Standardisation uses the mean and standard deviation, which outliers also distort.
The mansions are real data. Blind removal discards valid observations.

questions.question: Which order of steps avoids data leakage during preprocessing?
questions.explanation: Medians, scaling parameters and category mappings should be learned only from training data and then applied to the test data.
questions.concept: Split first, fit on train, transform both.
options: Split the data, fit preprocessing on the training set, then transform the training and test sets
Fit preprocessing on the full dataset, then split into training and test sets
Split the data, fit preprocessing on the test set, then transform the training set
Transform the test set first, then split and fit on the training set
whyWrong: Fitting on the full data lets the test set influence preprocessing parameters.
Fitting on the test set leaks it directly into training decisions.
Test data should only ever be transformed with parameters learned from training data.

questions.question: Fitting a scaler on the full dataset before splitting can leak information from the test set into training.
questions.explanation: The scaler's mean and standard deviation would include test rows, so the test set has indirectly influenced preprocessing.
questions.concept: Any statistic computed from test data is a leak.

questions.question: Scaling should be applied before cleaning and missing-value treatment.
questions.explanation: The lecture says scaling should be applied after cleaning and missing-value treatment.
questions.concept: Clean, impute and encode before scaling.

questions.question: Why does the lecture recommend building preprocessing as a pipeline?
questions.explanation: Pipelines bundle the steps so that parameters are fitted on training data and reused on test data in the same order every time.
questions.concept: Pipelines enforce the safe order automatically.
options: It removes the need to split the data into training and test sets
It always improves model accuracy
It replaces missing-value treatment
It makes the workflow reproducible and harder to misuse
whyWrong: A pipeline still needs a proper split; it enforces how fitting is done.
A pipeline is about correctness and reproducibility, not a guaranteed accuracy gain.
Imputation is one of the steps a pipeline contains.

questions.question: A team computes the median age on all 10,000 rows, imputes missing ages, standardises all features using the full dataset, then splits 80/20. Test accuracy is 91%, but accuracy on genuinely new data in production is 84%. What is the most likely explanation and fix?
questions.explanation: Fitting imputation and scaling on the full dataset lets the test set influence preprocessing parameters, which makes evaluation look better than it is. The safe order is split, fit on train, transform both.
questions.concept: Leakage makes evaluation optimistic.
options: The model is underfitting, so a more complex model is needed to close the production gap
Preprocessing saw the test rows, so the test score was optimistic; fit it on training data only
The median should have been replaced by the mean when imputing missing ages
Production data is always worse, so nothing in the workflow needs to change
whyWrong: The gap between test and production suggests an optimistic test estimate, not underfitting.
Changing the statistic does not fix the fact that it was computed on test data.
Some drift is possible, but the workflow contains a known leakage error that should be fixed.

questions.question: What is the main drawback of listwise deletion?
questions.explanation: Listwise deletion is easy but can shrink the dataset a lot. Deletion is more acceptable when missingness is small and plausibly random, and it must be reported.
questions.concept: Deletion changes the dataset used for analysis, so report it.
options: It removes whole columns that have high missingness from the dataset
It replaces missing values with the mean of each column
It adds an indicator column for every value that is missing
It drops every row with any gap and may discard many useful observations
whyWrong: That is column deletion, a different strategy.
That is mean imputation.
That is a missing indicator.

questions.question: Relevance, as a data-quality dimension, asks whether a variable helps answer the analysis question.
questions.explanation: Relevance is the sixth dimension in the lecture's table, alongside completeness, validity, consistency, uniqueness and timeliness.
questions.concept: Not every column helps answer the question.

questions.question: Why might an analyst add a missing indicator for a column even after imputing its missing values?
