questions.explanation: After imputation, a missing row looks like any other. A binary indicator keeps the information that the value was not recorded, which can be informative, though it should be used thoughtfully.
questions.concept: Imputation fills a gap; an indicator remembers that there was one.
options: Being missing may itself carry information that imputation hides
Because imputed values cannot be used by a model without an indicator
Because the indicator removes any bias that missingness causes
Because an indicator makes the imputed values exact
whyWrong: Models can use imputed values directly; the indicator adds information, it is not required.
The lecture warns that indicators may also encode collection bias.
Imputed values remain estimates whatever else is added.

questions.question: When a dataset is represented as a matrix X with n rows and p columns, what do n and p stand for?
questions.explanation: Each row of X is one sample (for example one student) and each column is one feature.
questions.concept: Rows are samples, columns are features, and y is kept separate.
options: n is the number of features; p is the number of samples
n is the number of targets; p is the number of predictions
n is the number of samples; p is the number of features
n is the number of models; p is the number of parameters
whyWrong: This reverses the convention: rows are samples, columns are features.
X holds the inputs only; the target y is separate.
X describes data, not models.

questions.question: Predicting a student's final grade on a numeric 0-20 scale is a classification task.
questions.explanation: Because the target is numeric and continuous, predicting it is a regression task. Classification predicts discrete labels such as pass/fail.
questions.concept: The type of target decides the type of task.

questions.question: What is a feature?
questions.explanation: Features can be numerical (age, absences), categorical (school) or ordinal (education level).
questions.concept: Features are the inputs; the target is the output.
options: A measurable property of the thing being observed, used as an input
The variable that the model is trying to predict from the inputs
One complete row of the dataset, such as one student
A weight that the model learns during training
whyWrong: That is the target, y.
A row is a sample; a feature is a column.
That is a model parameter.

questions.question: The lecture says 'garbage in, garbage out' and claims a simple linear model with well-engineered features can beat a complex model trained on raw data. What idea explains both statements?
questions.explanation: If the inputs carry no relevant signal, no algorithm can predict well. Features that express the underlying pattern let even simple models perform strongly.
questions.concept: Representation quality limits what any model can learn.
options: Complex models always overfit on tabular data, so simple models always win in practice
A model can only learn signal its features contain, so representation can matter more than the algorithm
Raw data contains no information at all until it has been scaled and encoded
Deep neural networks cannot be trained on tabular data, so simpler models are needed
whyWrong: The claim is about feature quality, not that complex models always lose.
Raw data contains information; the issue is whether it is represented usefully.
The lecture does not say this; it says even advanced algorithms need relevant signal.

questions.question: A bike-share company wants to predict hourly rental demand. Its raw data has a timestamp string for each rental and the GPS coordinates of each station. One analyst wants to feed the raw strings and coordinates directly into a model. Another proposes features such as 'is_weekend', 'hour_of_day' and 'distance to city centre'. Which reasoning best matches the lecture?
questions.explanation: Transforming time into weekend flags and GPS into distances turns raw data into features that reflect domain meaning, which is exactly what feature engineering aims to do.
questions.concept: Feature engineering re-expresses raw inputs so patterns are easier to learn.
options: Engineering is pointless, because any model extracts everything it needs from raw columns
Engineered features always remove information, so raw columns are the safer choice
Raw columns are not always the most informative form; engineered features expose the patterns directly
Feature engineering only applies to classification tasks, and rental demand is numeric
whyWrong: The lecture says raw columns are not always the most informative representation.
Good engineered features increase useful information by exposing patterns.
Feature engineering applies to regression tasks as well, such as predicting a grade.

questions.question: Match each method to what it does.
questions.explanation: All three change the feature space, in different ways: richer representation, smaller subset, or compressed space.
questions.concept: Create, choose, or compress.

pairs.right: Creates new features from existing ones
Keeps only a subset of the existing features
Builds new components as linear combinations of features

questions.question: Feature engineering, feature selection and PCA take place after basic cleaning and before model fitting.
questions.explanation: The lecture places this feature work between preprocessing and modelling.
questions.concept: Feature work sits between cleaning and modelling.

questions.question: In real projects, feature work is usually done once, in a single pass, before any evaluation.
questions.explanation: The lecture says feature work is usually iterative: inspect, transform, evaluate and revise.
questions.concept: Feature work is a loop, not a single step.

questions.question: A school wants a model with fewer inputs, and every input must be explainable to administrators in plain language. Which approach fits best, and why?
questions.explanation: The right method depends on the goal: meaning, relevance or compactness. Selection keeps original columns, so it suits explanation; PCA suits compression.
questions.concept: Choose the method that fits the purpose: explanation, prediction, visualisation or compression.
options: PCA, because components are always easier to explain than original variables
Feature selection, because it keeps original variables that remain directly interpretable
Feature engineering, because it always reduces the number of inputs
Keep all features, because removing any feature makes a model harder to explain
whyWrong: PCA components are weighted combinations, which usually reduces direct interpretability.
Engineering creates new features; it does not by itself reduce the count.
Fewer, original features make explanation easier, not harder.

questions.question: Three teams have different goals. Team A must compress 40 highly correlated sensor readings to plot machines in two dimensions. Team B's advisor wants to know which existing student attributes matter most, in plain terms. Team C needs to capture 'change in performance between two quizzes', which no single column shows. Which pairing is correct?
questions.explanation: PCA compresses correlated variables into a few components for visualisation. Selection keeps the most relevant original variables. Engineering creates a new variable such as a difference.
questions.concept: Compactness, relevance and meaning point to different methods.
options: A: feature selection; B: PCA; C: feature engineering
A: PCA; B: feature selection; C: feature engineering
A: PCA; B: feature engineering; C: feature selection
A: feature engineering; B: feature selection; C: PCA
whyWrong: Team B needs interpretable original attributes, which PCA does not give. Team A needs compression, which is PCA's strength.
Team C needs a new variable built from two columns; selection only keeps existing ones.
PCA builds variance-based components, not a meaningful 'change' feature; Team A's goal is compression.

questions.question: Feature engineering can be written as X_new = f(X_raw). Which requirement does the lecture place on the transformation f?
questions.explanation: A transformation that cannot be repeated, explained, or computed when a prediction is needed is not usable in practice.
questions.concept: Every engineered feature must be computable at prediction time.
options: It must always be nonlinear
It must use the target variable
It must increase the number of features as much as possible
It should be reproducible, documented and available at prediction time
whyWrong: f can be numeric, logical, categorical or domain-based; it need not be nonlinear.
Using the target in features causes leakage.
A good feature increases useful information, not just dimensionality.

questions.question: A good engineered feature should increase useful information, not simply increase the number of columns.
questions.explanation: The lecture says good features align with the real-world process and add information; adding columns without meaning adds noise.
questions.concept: More columns is not the same as more information.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a feature-engineering operation?
questions.explanation: Removing columns based on correlation is feature selection: it keeps a subset rather than creating new variables.
questions.concept: Engineering creates; selection removes.
options: Computing a ratio of two variables
Creating an interaction term between two variables
Recoding or grouping categories
Removing columns that have low correlation with the target
whyWrong: Ratios are an engineering operation.
Interactions are an engineering operation.
Recoding and grouping are listed engineering operations.

questions.question: A health model has raw 'height (m)' and 'weight (kg)' columns. Which engineered feature best expresses body size relative to height, in the spirit of the lecture's ratio features?
questions.explanation: A ratio feature expresses one quantity relative to another, which can be more informative than absolute values when context matters. Weight relative to height squared is the familiar body-mass index.
questions.concept: Ratios compare quantities on a common scale when the ratio has real meaning.
options: Weight plus height
Height minus weight
A one-hot encoding of height
Weight divided by height squared
whyWrong: Adding kilograms and metres has no meaningful interpretation.
Subtracting values in different units has no meaning.
One-hot encoding is for categories, not a continuous measurement.

questions.question: A university builds an early-warning model that runs in week 4 of the semester to flag students at risk of failing. The analyst includes 'final exam score' and 'absences in week 12' because both correlate strongly with failing. Accuracy in testing is excellent. What is wrong?
questions.explanation: Leakage occurs when a feature contains information not genuinely available at prediction time. For early intervention, later grades and outcomes are not permissible inputs.
questions.concept: Check every feature against the moment the prediction will be made.
options: Nothing: features with high correlation should always be kept
They are not available in week 4, so they leak future information
The features should be standardised, which would remove the problem
The two features should be combined with PCA so the model cannot see them directly
whyWrong: Correlation is not enough; a feature must be available when the prediction is made.
Scaling does not change when information becomes available.
Compressing leaked information still leaks it.

questions.question: What does an interaction feature model?
questions.explanation: Multiplying two variables lets a linear model capture a conditional relationship without needing a fully nonlinear model.
questions.concept: Interactions capture 'it depends'.
options: That the effect of one variable depends on another variable
The average of two related variables measured at the same time
The square of a single variable, used to model curvature
The difference between two measurements taken at different times
whyWrong: An average is a summary feature, not an interaction.
A squared term is a polynomial feature.
A difference captures change, not dependence of one effect on another.

questions.question: A difference feature such as (second test score - first test score) equal to 0 tells you the student is performing well.
questions.explanation: A value of 0 means stability, but a student stable at a high score and a student stable at a low score both get 0. The feature should be read alongside a level feature.
questions.concept: A change feature needs a level feature for context.

questions.question: A salesperson sold 40 units in quarter 1 and 52 units in quarter 2. What is the value of a 'progress' feature defined as Q2 - Q1, and what does its sign suggest?
questions.explanation: A positive difference suggests improvement, negative suggests decline and zero suggests stability.
questions.concept: A difference feature captures momentum.
options: -12, suggesting decline
+12, suggesting improvement
92, suggesting strong performance
46, suggesting average performance
whyWrong: Q2 - Q1 = 52 - 40, which is positive.
92 is the sum, not the difference.
46 is the average of the two quarters.

questions.question: Why can an average of two early grades be a more useful feature than either grade alone?
questions.explanation: Summary features reduce variance and short-term fluctuation. Keeping both raw and summary features can still be useful.
questions.concept: Summaries trade detail for stability.
options: Because an average always correlates perfectly with the final grade
It reflects sustained achievement and is less affected by one unusual test
Because the original grades must be deleted once the average exists
Because averaging removes the need for a separate train-test split
whyWrong: No feature correlates perfectly; the average is more stable, not perfect.
The lecture says the average should not automatically replace the raw features.
Feature design does not replace evaluation practice.

questions.question: An analyst creates 'absences_per_point = absences / prior_score', where prior_score can be 0, and also adds interaction terms for every pair of 25 variables. Several students now have extremely large feature values, and the model performs worse on new data. What is the best critique?
questions.explanation: Ratios must be used carefully because small denominators create instability; the lecture's example adds 1 to the denominator. Too many interactions inflate complexity, so a small justified set is better.
questions.concept: Engineer features that are stable and meaningful, not as many as possible.
questions.source: Lec 3.1, slide 27, Lec 3.1, slide 28, Lec 3.1, slide 42
options: Tiny denominators make the ratio unstable, and so many interactions invite overfitting
The model needs even more interaction terms to cancel out the extreme ratio values
Extreme ratio values are genuine outliers and should be kept unchanged in the model
The only problem is that the new features were not one-hot encoded before training
whyWrong: More interactions increase complexity and overfitting further.
These extremes come from tiny denominators in the feature design, not from real behaviour.
These are numeric features; one-hot encoding does not apply.

questions.question: Adding a squared term such as x² lets a linear model represent curvature in a relationship.
questions.explanation: Polynomial features let a simple model behave more flexibly in the original feature space.
questions.concept: New nonlinear features let linear models fit curves.

questions.question: What is the main risk of adding many polynomial features?
questions.explanation: Polynomial features should be used selectively because more flexible representations can overfit if not well justified.
questions.concept: Flexibility costs stability.
options: They make the model unable to represent any curved relationship
They convert numeric features into categories that need encoding
They can amplify noise and multicollinearity, leading to overfitting
They remove the need to keep a separate test set for evaluation
whyWrong: They add curvature; that is their purpose.
Polynomial terms remain numeric.
No feature type removes the need for evaluation.

questions.question: A university dataset has the variables below. Match each to a suitable treatment.
questions.explanation: Binary variables become 0/1, nominal variables get one indicator per category, ordinal variables keep their order with a stated assumption, and numeric features stay numeric.
questions.concept: Encoding depends on whether a category is binary, nominal or ordinal.

pairs.right: Binary 0/1
One-hot encoding
Keep the order, stating the spacing assumption
Keep as a numeric feature

questions.question: Why does the lecture say strong engineered features usually come from domain knowledge rather than blind trial and error?
questions.explanation: A useful question is what a teacher or advisor would consider informative. Features grounded in the real process are easier to justify and explain.
questions.concept: Start from domain meaning.
options: They are plausible, interpretable and defensible, while arbitrary features add noise
Domain knowledge guarantees higher accuracy than any automated feature method
Features found by trial and error cannot be computed reliably in Python
Domain knowledge removes the need to check engineered features for leakage
whyWrong: The lecture argues for plausibility and interpretability, not a guaranteed accuracy win.
They can be computed; the problem is that they often lack meaning.
Leakage checks are still needed for every feature.

questions.question: A linear model predicts exam score from weekly study hours. Plots show that scores rise steadily up to about 15 hours and then level off, and the model's errors follow a clear curved pattern. Which change best follows the lecture?
questions.explanation: A squared term lets a linear model bend. It should be justified and checked, because more flexible representations can overfit.
questions.concept: Use the simplest nonlinear feature that captures the pattern.
options: Replace the model with a very large neural network, because linear models cannot be fixed
Add terms up to the 10th power of study hours to capture every detail
Add a squared study-hours term, then check it improves results on held-out data
Drop study hours, because its relationship with the score is not linear
whyWrong: The lecture shows that engineered nonlinear features let simple models capture curvature.
High-degree terms amplify noise and overfit; polynomial features should be used selectively.
A nonlinear relationship is still a relationship; removing the feature discards signal.

questions.question: Match each kind of problematic feature to its description.
questions.explanation: The lecture warns about constant, sparse and overly specific features, and says leaking features are the most dangerous.
questions.concept: Bad features add no signal, add noise, or add false signal.

pairs.right: Every row has the same value (variance 0)
Almost all rows are 0 or empty
Too specific to the training set, such as a student ID
Contains information not available when predicting

questions.question: A feature whose value is the same in every row gives the model useful variation to learn from.
questions.explanation: A constant feature has variance 0, so it gives the model nothing to distinguish samples by.
questions.concept: No variation, no information.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a characteristic of a good feature listed in the lecture?
questions.explanation: Good features have high correlation with the target, low redundancy, are model-agnostic and computationally efficient.
questions.concept: Low redundancy is part of being a good feature.
options: It relates closely to the target the model is predicting
It repeats information already contained in other columns
It works across many different types of algorithms
It is cheap and easy to calculate at prediction time
whyWrong: High correlation with the target is listed.
Being model-agnostic is listed.
Computational efficiency is listed.

questions.question: A bank predicts which loans will default. One feature is 'collection agency assigned', which is set only after a customer stops paying. What problem does this feature create?
questions.explanation: A feature that is only known after the outcome is a form of leakage and produces unrealistically high accuracy.
questions.concept: Ask whether the feature exists before the outcome is known.
options: Target leakage, because it is only known after default
Multicollinearity, because it is correlated with income
Sparsity, because most of its values are zero
Low variance, because it only has two possible values
whyWrong: The issue is timing, not correlation with another predictor.
Even if it were sparse, the decisive problem is that it reveals the outcome.
Binary features can be perfectly valid; this one is invalid because of timing.

questions.question: A model predicting each student's final numeric course score reaches almost perfect accuracy. Its features include study hours, attendance, a 'letter grade' column (A to F, assigned from the final score) and the student ID number. What explains the result, and what should change?
questions.explanation: Using the target, or a transformation of it, to predict the target is leakage. Identifiers are overly specific to the training set and lead to overfitting.
questions.concept: Unrealistically high accuracy is a warning sign for leakage.
questions.source: Lec 3.1, slide 38, Lec 3.1, slide 39, Lec 3.1, slide 42
options: The model is excellent and should be deployed as it is
Only the student ID should be removed, because letter grades are a normal feature
The letter grade should be one-hot encoded so the model uses it correctly
The letter grade leaks the target and the ID is too specific; remove both
whyWrong: Near-perfect accuracy here comes from leakage, not real predictive power.
The letter grade is derived from the target itself, which is direct leakage.
Encoding a leaked feature still leaks the target.

questions.question: What is feature selection?
questions.explanation: Unlike engineering, selection does not change the data; it decides which columns to keep.
questions.concept: Selection keeps; it does not transform.
options: Creating new columns by combining or transforming existing ones
Rotating the data onto new orthogonal axes called components
Choosing which existing columns to keep, without changing them
Filling in missing values in the columns that will be kept
whyWrong: That is feature engineering.
That is PCA.
That is imputation.

questions.question: Match each family of feature-selection methods to its description.
questions.explanation: Filters such as correlation screening are fast first passes. Wrappers search subsets with a model. Embedded methods select while training.
questions.concept: Filter before, wrapper around, embedded inside the model.

pairs.right: Statistical screening; fast
Tries subsets of features using a model; iterative and accurate
Selection happens inside model training, as in regularisation

questions.question: Feature selection can make training and prediction faster and make models easier to explain.
questions.explanation: The lecture lists speed, explainability and robustness against overfitting as benefits.
questions.concept: Fewer, better features: faster, clearer, more robust.

questions.question: A feature that seems irrelevant by itself can become useful in combination with other features, so selection needs judgment rather than a purely mechanical rule.
questions.explanation: The lecture says a feature may appear irrelevant alone but be useful in interaction with others, so selection is a decision aid.
questions.concept: Individual screening can miss interactions.

questions.question: A model predicting household energy use includes 'floor area in m²', 'floor area in ft²', 'house colour' and 'insulation rating'. The linear model's coefficients for the two area columns change wildly between training runs. What is the best action?
questions.explanation: Redundant features carry overlapping information and lead to unstable coefficient estimates in linear models. Selection keeps the most representative variables and removes overlap.
questions.concept: Redundancy destabilises linear models.
options: Keep all four columns, because more features always give a model more information
Remove insulation rating, because ordinal ratings make coefficients unstable
Keep one floor-area column, check house colour for signal, and keep insulation rating
Apply PCA to house colour alone to stabilise the two area coefficients
whyWrong: Redundant features carry the same information and make coefficients unstable.
Ordinal features can be highly relevant; the instability comes from the area columns.
The instability comes from the duplicated area columns, not from colour.

questions.question: A feature has a Pearson correlation of -0.85 with the target. What does this indicate?
questions.explanation: Pearson r lies between -1 and +1. The sign gives the direction, and the magnitude |r| gives the strength.
questions.concept: Read r by sign for direction and |r| for strength.
options: No relationship, because the value is negative
A weak positive association
A strong negative linear association
A strong nonlinear relationship
whyWrong: A negative value indicates direction, not absence of a relationship.
The sign is negative and the magnitude is large.
Pearson correlation measures linear association only.

questions.question: A correlation coefficient near zero proves there is no relationship of any kind between two variables.
questions.explanation: A value near zero suggests a weak linear association. Correlation can miss nonlinear relationships.
questions.concept: Pearson r measures only linear association.

questions.question: Features with extremely low variance are common candidates for removal.
questions.explanation: If values barely vary, the model has little variability to learn from. The decision should still consider domain understanding.
questions.concept: Low variance means little information.

questions.question: Why are features usually ranked by |r| (the absolute value of the correlation) rather than by r itself?
questions.explanation: Selection focuses on the strength of association. The sign shows only direction, and either direction can carry predictive signal.
questions.concept: Strength matters for selection; direction matters for interpretation.
options: A strong negative relationship is as useful for prediction as a strong positive one
Negative correlations are always caused by data errors
Taking the absolute value turns a nonlinear relationship into a linear one
Because r cannot be negative for numeric features
whyWrong: Negative correlations are often real, for example more failures with lower grades.
Absolute value does not change the type of relationship.
r ranges from -1 to +1.

questions.question: An analysis finds that 'number of library visits' has r = 0.6 with final grades, while 'hours of sleep' has r = 0.05. The administration proposes requiring library visits to raise grades and wants to drop sleep from the model. Which response best reflects the lecture?
questions.explanation: Common mistakes include treating correlation as causation and removing variables only because their individual correlation is small. Filters are a first screen, combined with domain reasoning.
questions.concept: Association is not causation, and screening is not a final verdict.
options: Correlation is not causation, and a weak individual correlation does not prove sleep is useless
Agree with both proposals, because correlation shows which variables cause the outcome
Drop library visits instead, because high correlations usually indicate leakage
Keep sleep in the model only if its correlation with grades turns out to be negative
whyWrong: The lecture warns against confusing correlation with causation.
High correlation can indicate leakage, but here visits occur before the outcome; the issue is causal interpretation.
The sign does not decide relevance; the limits of linear screening do.

questions.question: What is Principal Component Analysis (PCA)?
questions.explanation: PCA finds new axes (principal components) that capture as much variation as possible with fewer dimensions.
questions.concept: PCA rotates and projects the data.
options: A supervised method that keeps the features most correlated with the target
A method for filling in missing values using nearby rows
A nonlinear method that learns neural network representations
A linear technique that turns features into fewer orthogonal components
whyWrong: That describes correlation-based feature selection; PCA is usually unsupervised.
That is imputation.
PCA is linear; nonlinear methods such as UMAP are listed as future topics.

questions.question: The second principal component can point in the same direction as the first if variance remains in that direction.
questions.explanation: The second component captures the next largest remaining variance while staying orthogonal to the first.
questions.concept: Components are orthogonal, so they never duplicate a direction.

questions.question: Match each PCA term to its meaning.
questions.explanation: Eigenvectors of the covariance matrix give directions, eigenvalues give variance, loadings are the feature weights, and the explained variance ratio and scree plot help choose k.
questions.concept: Direction, size and weight: eigenvector, eigenvalue, loading.
questions.source: Lec 3.1, slide 58, Lec 3.1, slide 60, Lec 3.1, slide 61

pairs.right: Weight of a feature in a component
Direction of a principal component
Amount of variance captured along a component
Fraction of total variance a component captures
Chart of each component's decreasing contribution

questions.question: Why is standardisation usually essential before PCA?
questions.explanation: Because PCA looks for directions of maximum variance, a feature measured in large units would capture most of the variance purely because of its scale.
questions.concept: Scale first so variance reflects structure, not units.
options: PCA cannot run on values that are not already between 0 and 1
PCA follows variance, so large-range features would dominate the components
Standardisation turns PCA into a supervised method that uses the target
Standardisation removes the need to choose how many components to keep
whyWrong: PCA runs on any numeric data; scaling is about fairness between features.
Scaling does not involve the target.
k must still be chosen, for example from explained variance.

questions.question: An analyst applies PCA to annual income (in dollars), age (in years) and number of children without scaling. PC1 loads almost entirely on income. The analyst reports that 'PC1 represents overall prosperity and life stage'. What is the best critique?
questions.explanation: Applying PCA before standardisation lets large-scale variables dominate. PC1 should be interpreted from its actual loadings, not assumed.
questions.concept: Standardise, then inspect loadings before naming a component.
options: Income dominates only because of its units; standardise first, then read PC1's loadings
The interpretation is correct, because PC1 always represents an overall summary of all features
Age and number of children should be removed because they did not appear in PC1
PCA should be fitted separately on each feature
whyWrong: PC1 must not be assumed to mean anything without checking its loadings.
They did not appear because of scale, not because they lack structure.
PCA needs the features together to find shared directions.

questions.question: What is the explained variance ratio mainly used for in PCA?
questions.explanation: The explained variance ratio shows what fraction of total variance each component captures, which guides the choice of k.
questions.concept: Keep enough components to explain enough of the variance for the task.
options: Choosing which rows to delete
Measuring correlation with the target
Deciding how many components to retain
Encoding categorical variables
whyWrong: PCA does not remove rows.
PCA usually does not use the target.
Encoding is a separate preprocessing step.

questions.question: PCA loadings show the causal effect of each feature on the outcome.
questions.explanation: Loadings summarise covariance structure in the data; they do not represent causal effects.
questions.concept: Loadings describe structure, not causes.

questions.question: In a covariance matrix, the diagonal entries are variances and the off-diagonal entries are covariances.
questions.explanation: The covariance matrix summarises how variables vary together; PCA solves an eigenvalue problem on it.
questions.concept: Diagonal: variance; off-diagonal: covariance.

questions.question: PCA on five standardised features gives explained variance ratios of 0.55, 0.25, 0.12, 0.05 and 0.03. What is the smallest number of components that explains at least 90% of the variance?
questions.explanation: Cumulative variance: 0.55, then 0.80, then 0.92. Three components are the first to pass 90%.
questions.concept: Add explained variance ratios until the cumulative total reaches the target.
whyWrong: The first two components explain 0.55 + 0.25 = 0.80, which is below 0.90.
Three components already reach 0.92, so four are not the minimum.
The first component explains only 0.55.

questions.question: PCA on standardised student data gives PC1 = 0.60 × attendance + 0.50 × homework completion - 0.45 × late submissions + 0.05 × age. A student has a very high PC1 score. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: A positive loading means the component increases with that feature; a negative loading means it decreases. Interpretation is based on the largest-magnitude loadings and is not causal.
questions.concept: Read loadings by sign and magnitude, and never as causes.
options: The student probably has many late submissions, because that loading is large
PC1 mainly measures age, because age appears in the equation
Raising PC1 will cause the student's final grade to improve
High attendance and homework completion, few late submissions; age matters little
whyWrong: The late-submissions loading is negative, so a high PC1 goes with fewer late submissions.
Age's loading (0.05) is the smallest; interpretation follows the largest magnitudes.
Loadings summarise covariance structure; they do not describe causal effects.

questions.question: Which practice is a mistake when using PCA in a model-evaluation workflow?
questions.explanation: Full-data PCA lets the test set influence the components, which leaks information. PCA should be fitted on training data only.
questions.concept: Every fitted transformation, PCA included, is fitted on training data only.
options: Standardising the features before applying PCA
Inspecting loadings before naming a component
Using explained variance to choose the number of components
Fitting PCA on the full dataset before splitting it
whyWrong: Standardising first is the recommended practice.
Inspecting loadings is recommended.
This is the recommended way to choose k.

questions.question: Feature selection usually keeps interpretability high, while PCA often lowers direct interpretability.
questions.explanation: Selection keeps original variables; PCA creates weighted combinations that are harder to interpret directly.
questions.concept: Selection keeps meaning; PCA trades meaning for compactness.

questions.question: Why can PCA help when a dataset has strongly correlated (multicollinear) features?
questions.explanation: Correlated features carry overlapping information. PCA re-expresses them as orthogonal components ordered by variance, which removes the duplication.
questions.concept: Orthogonal components cannot overlap.
options: Because PCA deletes every feature that is correlated with another
Because PCA uses the target to choose which correlated feature to keep
Because PCA makes every feature's variance exactly equal to 1
Its components are orthogonal, so they do not duplicate the same direction of variation
whyWrong: PCA does not delete features; it combines them into new components.
PCA is usually unsupervised and does not use the target.
That describes standardisation, not PCA.

questions.question: A photo app attaches every tag that applies to a picture, such as 'beach', 'sunset' and 'family' at the same time. What type of classification is this?
questions.explanation: Multi-label classification assigns several labels to one instance, like tagging a photo with more than one tag.
questions.concept: Count how many labels one instance can receive.
options: Binary classification
Multiclass classification
Multi-label classification
Regression
whyWrong: Binary classification chooses one of exactly two classes.
Multiclass assigns exactly one label from more than two classes.
Regression predicts a continuous number, not labels.

questions.question: Classification maps input features to a continuous numeric output.
questions.explanation: Classification maps inputs to a discrete set of categorical labels. Continuous outputs are the job of regression.
questions.concept: Classification outputs categories; regression outputs numbers.

questions.question: Match each step of the classification workflow to what happens in it.
questions.explanation: The workflow moves from preparing data, to choosing predictors, to training, to evaluating on data the model has not seen.
questions.concept: Prepare, select, train, evaluate.

pairs.right: Handle missing values and encode variables
Identify relevant predictors
Train the classifier on labelled data
Test on unseen data using metrics

questions.question: Why is a classifier evaluated on a test set that was not used for training?
questions.explanation: A model can memorise training data. Testing on unseen data shows how it will perform on new cases.
questions.concept: Judge a model on data it has never seen.
options: Because the training set is too small to compute accuracy on
To estimate performance on new data, since training performance is optimistic
Because the test set contains the most important classes
Because scikit-learn cannot evaluate a model on its training data
whyWrong: Accuracy can be computed on any set; the point is to measure generalisation.
A test set is a held-out sample, not a set of special classes.
It is possible; it just gives an over-optimistic result.

questions.question: A news platform needs three models. (a) Assign each article exactly one section: sport, politics, technology or health. (b) Mark each reader comment as spam or not spam. (c) Attach any number of the tags 'video', 'breaking', 'opinion' and 'local' to each article. Which description is correct?
questions.explanation: Binary has two exclusive classes, multiclass has more than two exclusive classes, and multi-label allows several labels per instance.
questions.concept: Ask: how many classes, and can an instance have more than one?
options: (a) multi-label, (b) binary, (c) multiclass
(a) multiclass, (b) multiclass, (c) multi-label
(a) binary, (b) binary, (c) multiclass
(a) multiclass, (b) binary, (c) multi-label
whyWrong: Each article gets exactly one section in (a), and (c) allows several tags at once.
Spam vs not spam has exactly two exclusive classes, so it is binary.
(a) has four classes, and (c) allows more than one label per article.

questions.question: What is the output of the sigmoid function when its input z = 0?
questions.explanation: sigmoid(z) = 1 / (1 + e^-z). At z = 0, e^0 = 1, so the output is 1/2.
questions.concept: z = 0 sits exactly on the decision boundary.
whyWrong: The sigmoid approaches 0 only as z becomes very negative.
The sigmoid approaches 1 only as z becomes very positive.
The sigmoid's output never goes below 0.

questions.question: The sigmoid function maps any real-valued input to a value between 0 and 1, which can be read as a probability.
questions.explanation: Logistic regression applies the sigmoid to the linear output so that predictions are probabilities.
questions.concept: Sigmoid turns a score into a probability.

questions.question: What does logistic regression model as a linear combination of the features?
questions.explanation: The logit, the inverse of the sigmoid, is the log of the odds. Logistic regression models it as a linear function, so a coefficient is the change in log-odds per unit change in its feature.
questions.concept: Linear in log-odds, sigmoid to probability.
options: The probability itself, directly
The squared error
The log-odds of the positive class
The class label as 0 or 1 directly
whyWrong: The probability comes from applying the sigmoid to the linear combination.
Squared error is a regression cost, not what is modelled.
Fitting labels directly with a linear model is the problem logistic regression avoids.

questions.question: Why is linear regression a poor choice for a classification task?
questions.explanation: Linear regression is designed for continuous values, so its outputs are not valid probabilities, and extreme points move the line.
questions.concept: Classification needs bounded probabilities.
options: It cannot be trained on numeric features, only on categorical ones
Its outputs are not bounded between 0 and 1, and outliers shift the boundary
It always produces exactly 0 or 1, so it gives no probabilities
It needs the sigmoid function during training, which is too slow
whyWrong: Linear regression is trained on numeric features.
It produces continuous values, which is the problem.
Linear regression does not use a sigmoid; logistic regression does.

questions.question: A fraud model computes z = 0.8 × x1 - 1.2 × x2 + 0.4. For a transaction with x1 = 2 and x2 = 1, a junior analyst writes two claims in a report. Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: z = 0.8 × 2 - 1.2 × 1 + 0.4 = 0.8. sigmoid(0.8) = 1 / (1 + e^-0.8), about 0.69, which is above 0.5. Coefficients act on log-odds.
questions.concept: Compute z, apply the sigmoid, compare with 0.5, and interpret coefficients in log-odds.
questions.source: Lec 4.1, slide 9, Lec 4.1, slide 10, Lec 4.1, slide 12
options: z = 0.8, so the probability of fraud is exactly 0.8 and it is flagged
z = 0.8 is below 1, so the transaction is classified as not fraud
Raising x2 by 1 lowers the probability of fraud by exactly 1.2
p ≈ 0.69, so it is flagged as fraud; x2 lowers the log-odds by 1.2 per unit
whyWrong: z is the log-odds, not the probability. The sigmoid must be applied.
The boundary is z = 0 (probability 0.5), not z = 1.
A probability cannot change by 1.2; the coefficient changes the log-odds.

questions.question: Logistic regression uses mean squared error as its cost function because MSE is convex for logistic outputs.
questions.explanation: MSE is non-convex for logistic regression, so binary cross-entropy (log loss) is used instead.
questions.concept: Logistic regression is trained with log loss.

questions.question: Under log loss, what happens when the true label is 1 but the model predicts a probability close to 0?
questions.explanation: Log loss heavily punishes confident wrong predictions, which pushes the model toward well-calibrated probabilities.
questions.concept: Confident mistakes cost the most.
options: The cost becomes 0
The cost is capped at 1
The example is ignored during training
The cost becomes very large
whyWrong: Cost is 0 only when the prediction matches the label confidently.
Log loss is not capped; it grows without bound as the prediction approaches the wrong extreme.
Every example contributes to the cost.

questions.question: The gradient-descent update for logistic regression has the same form as the update for linear regression.
questions.explanation: The lecture notes that the update rule looks identical: theta is reduced by alpha times the gradient X^T(y_pred - y)/m, where y_pred now comes from the sigmoid.
questions.concept: Same update form; different prediction function.

questions.question: A logistic regression model has weights w = [0.5, -0.25] and bias b = 0. What probability does it output for x = [1.0, 2.0]?
questions.concept: Forward pass: dot product plus bias, then sigmoid.
whyWrong: This would need z to be about 0.5, but 0.5 × 1.0 - 0.25 × 2.0 = 0.
A sigmoid output of exactly 0 would need z to be minus infinity.
A sigmoid output of exactly 1 would need z to be plus infinity.

questions.question: A bank must explain to regulators why each loan application is rejected. The data are tabular and the relationship between features and default appears roughly linear. The team needs a first model that is fast and easy to interpret. Which choice best fits the lecture?
questions.explanation: The lecture lists logistic regression's strengths as interpretable coefficients, efficiency on linear data, and use as a baseline for classification.
questions.concept: Start with an interpretable baseline before adding complexity.
options: K-nearest neighbours, because it has no training phase
An unconstrained decision tree grown until every leaf is pure
XGBoost first, because it wins most competitions
Logistic regression as an interpretable, efficient baseline
whyWrong: KNN stores the whole training set and gives no coefficients to explain decisions.
Unpruned trees overfit and become hard to justify as a stable rule set.
Boosted ensembles can be accurate but are less directly interpretable; the lecture presents logistic regression as the baseline.

questions.question: Why is KNN called a 'lazy learner'?
questions.explanation: KNN is lazy and non-parametric: it keeps all training data and makes decisions at inference time.
questions.concept: KNN learns nothing up front; it compares at prediction time.
options: It needs fewer features than other classification models
It always predicts the majority class of the training set
It only ever looks at one neighbour when it predicts
It stores the training data and does its work only at prediction time
whyWrong: Laziness refers to when computation happens, not feature count.
KNN predicts from the nearest neighbours, not the overall majority.
K can be any value.

questions.question: What is the Euclidean distance between the points (1, 2) and (4, 6)?
questions.explanation: Euclidean distance = sqrt((4-1)² + (6-2)²) = sqrt(9 + 16) = 5.
questions.concept: Euclidean is straight-line distance.
whyWrong: 7 is the Manhattan distance: |4-1| + |6-2|.
25 is the squared distance before taking the square root.
This is not produced by either distance formula.

questions.question: Manhattan distance is computed by summing the absolute differences of the coordinates.
questions.explanation: Manhattan (L1, city-block) distance adds |p_i - q_i| across all dimensions.
questions.concept: Manhattan moves along the grid; Euclidean cuts across.

questions.question: For the points p = (1, 2, 3) and q = (4, 0, 3), which pair of values is correct?
questions.explanation: Differences are 3, 2 and 0. Manhattan = 3 + 2 + 0 = 5. Euclidean = sqrt(9 + 4 + 0) = sqrt(13), about 3.61.
questions.concept: Sum absolute differences for L1; square-root the sum of squares for L2.
options: Manhattan = 5, Euclidean ≈ 3.61
Manhattan = 3.61, Euclidean = 5
Manhattan = 13, Euclidean ≈ 3.61
Manhattan = 5, Euclidean = 13
whyWrong: The values are swapped: Manhattan is 3 + 2 + 0 = 5.
13 is the squared Euclidean distance (9 + 4 + 0).
13 must be square-rooted to give the Euclidean distance.

questions.question: A fruit-sorting machine uses KNN with K = 3 on two scaled features (sweetness, crunchiness). Training points: A (1, 2) red, B (2, 4) blue, C (3, 3) blue, D (5, 5) red, E (2, 1) red. A new fruit is measured at (2, 2). Using Euclidean distance, what does the machine predict?
questions.explanation: Distances from (2, 2): A = 1, E = 1, C ≈ 1.41, B = 2, D ≈ 4.24. The three nearest are red, red and blue, so the majority vote is red.
questions.concept: Compute every distance, take the K smallest, then vote.
questions.source: Lec 4.1, slide 16, Lec 4.1, slide 17, Lec 4.1, slide 21
options: Red, because the three nearest points are A, E (both red) and C (blue)
Blue, because two of the three nearest points are blue
Blue, because C is the single closest point
No prediction is possible, because KNN must be trained first
whyWrong: B is at distance 2, farther than A and E (distance 1 each). The nearest three are A, E and C.
C is at about 1.41; A and E are closer at exactly 1.
KNN needs no training phase; it decides at prediction time.

questions.question: Why is an odd value of K recommended for binary classification?
questions.explanation: With two classes and an odd number of voters, one class always wins.
questions.concept: Odd K, no ties.
options: Because even values of K cannot be computed
To avoid ties in the vote
Because odd K always gives higher accuracy
Because odd K removes the need for scaling
whyWrong: Even K values can be computed; they just allow ties.
Odd K prevents ties; it does not guarantee higher accuracy.
Scaling is still required for distance-based models.

questions.question: A very small K, such as K = 1, gives a smooth decision boundary and high bias.
questions.explanation: Small K gives a complex boundary, high sensitivity to outliers and high variance (overfitting). Large K gives a smooth boundary and high bias.
questions.concept: Small K overfits; large K underfits.

questions.question: Scaling is essential for KNN because a feature with a much larger range would dominate the distance.
questions.explanation: The lecture's example: income from $0 to $1M would overshadow age from 18 to 90 entirely.
questions.concept: Distance-based models need comparable feature scales.

questions.question: Why does KNN struggle when the number of features becomes very large?
questions.explanation: As dimensions increase, volume grows exponentially, points become equidistant, and much more data is needed to keep density. Dimensionality reduction such as PCA helps.
questions.concept: In high dimensions, 'near' and 'far' blur together.
options: KNN cannot store more than a few features in memory
Points become almost equally distant, so 'nearest' stops meaning local
More features always remove the need for scaling
KNN automatically switches to Manhattan distance in high dimensions
whyWrong: Memory grows, but the core problem is that distances lose meaning.
Scaling is still needed; more features make the problem worse.
No automatic switch happens.

questions.question: A KNN churn model uses income (range $0 to $1,000,000), number of support calls (0 to 10) and 300 one-hot product columns. Accuracy is poor, and nearly every prediction seems driven by income. Which plan best follows the lecture?
questions.explanation: Unscaled large-range features dominate distance, and very many dimensions make neighbours less meaningful. Scaling, dimensionality reduction and K tuning address both.
questions.concept: Fix scale and dimensionality before tuning anything else in KNN.
questions.source: Lec 4.1, slide 19, Lec 4.1, slide 23, Lec 4.1, slide 24
options: Set K = 1 so that the model captures more local detail
Add more one-hot columns so the model has more information
Scale the features, reduce the dimensionality and then tune K
Skip scaling, because KNN is non-parametric and has no weights
whyWrong: K = 1 increases variance and does nothing about scale or dimensionality.
More dimensions worsen the curse of dimensionality.
Non-parametric does not mean scale-free; distances depend directly on feature ranges.

questions.question: Label the parts of a decision tree: match each term to its role.
questions.explanation: A tree splits data by feature tests from the root through internal nodes to leaves. Pruning keeps it from growing until it memorises noise.
questions.concept: Trees ask questions from the root down to answers at the leaves.

pairs.right: The top-level split
A later decision based on a feature test
A predicted outcome
Limiting or removing branches to reduce overfitting

questions.question: A node contains 6 samples of class A and 2 samples of class B. What is its Gini impurity?
questions.concept: Gini = 1 - sum of squared class proportions.
whyWrong: 0.25 is the proportion of class B, not the impurity.
0.625 is the sum of squared proportions (0.5625 + 0.0625); Gini is 1 minus that.
0.5 is the Gini impurity of a perfectly balanced two-class node.

questions.question: A node with entropy 0 is perfectly mixed between classes.
questions.explanation: Entropy 0 means the node is perfectly pure (all one class). For two balanced classes, entropy is 1.
questions.concept: Entropy measures disorder: 0 pure, 1 maximally mixed for two classes.

questions.question: Why does an unconstrained decision tree tend to overfit?
questions.explanation: Pre-pruning (max_depth, min_samples_split, min_samples_leaf) or post-pruning limits growth so the tree learns general patterns.
questions.concept: Purity at every leaf usually means memorisation.
options: It splits until every leaf is pure, so it models noise in the training data
It cannot split on numeric features, so it memorises categories
It stops after a single split, which makes it memorise the data
It uses Gini instead of entropy, which is known to overfit
whyWrong: Trees split on numeric and categorical features.
That describes a stump, which underfits rather than overfits.
Gini and entropy usually give similar results; neither causes overfitting by itself.

questions.question: A loan-approval tree is choosing its next split. The parent node is a 50/50 mix (entropy 1.0). Split A produces two equal-sized children, each with entropy 0.9. Split B produces two equal-sized children with entropies 0.0 and 0.8. Using information gain, which split should be chosen?
questions.explanation: IG = parent entropy - weighted child entropy. Split A: 1.0 - 0.9 = 0.1. Split B: 1.0 - (0.5 × 0.0 + 0.5 × 0.8) = 0.6. The tree picks the split with the highest information gain.
questions.concept: Choose the split that reduces disorder the most.
options: Split A, because its children are equally mixed and therefore balanced
Split A, because higher child entropy means more information gained
Neither, because a split is only valid if all children have entropy 0
Split B, with information gain 0.6 compared with 0.1 for split A
whyWrong: Balanced impurity is not the goal; the reduction in entropy is.
Information gain is the reduction in entropy; higher child entropy means less gain.
Splits rarely produce perfectly pure children; the best split has the highest gain.

questions.question: A confusion matrix has four cells. Match each cell to what it counts.
questions.explanation: The first word says whether the prediction was right; the second says what was predicted.
questions.concept: Right or wrong, then predicted positive or negative.

pairs.right: Predicted positive, actually positive
Predicted negative, actually negative
Predicted positive, actually negative
Predicted negative, actually positive

questions.question: Which question does precision answer?
questions.explanation: Precision = TP / (TP + FP). Recall = TP / (TP + FN).
questions.concept: Precision looks at predicted positives; recall looks at actual positives.
options: When the model predicts positive, how often is it right?
Of all actual positives, how many did the model find?
What fraction of all predictions were correct?
How well does the model separate the classes across all thresholds?
whyWrong: That is recall (sensitivity).
That is accuracy.
That is ROC-AUC.

questions.question: An AUC of 0.5 means the classifier separates the classes no better than random guessing.
questions.explanation: AUC = 1 means perfect separation; AUC = 0.5 means no better than random.
questions.concept: AUC summarises separation across all thresholds.

questions.question: A classifier's confusion matrix has TP = 40, FP = 10, FN = 20 and TN = 930. Which pair of values is correct?
questions.concept: Precision divides by predicted positives; recall divides by actual positives.
options: Precision ≈ 0.67, recall = 0.80
Precision = 0.97, recall = 0.80
Precision = 0.80, recall ≈ 0.67
Precision = 0.80, recall = 0.97
whyWrong: The values are swapped. Precision uses FP: 40/50. Recall uses FN: 40/60.
0.97 is accuracy, (40 + 930) / 1000, not precision.
0.97 is accuracy, not recall.

questions.question: A screening model for a rare condition (1% of patients) predicts 'healthy' for every patient and reports 99% accuracy. The hospital wants to deploy it. What is the best evaluation response?
questions.explanation: With 99% negatives, predicting the majority class gives 99% accuracy and zero recall. F1, per-class metrics in the classification report, and AUC reveal the problem.
questions.concept: On imbalanced data, look beyond accuracy.
options: Deploy it, because 99% accuracy is an excellent result for any screening model
Report precision alone, because it is the most important metric for screening
Increase the test set size until the measured accuracy reaches 100%
Accuracy hides the imbalance: recall is 0, so check per-class metrics, F1 and AUC
whyWrong: The model never detects a single case; accuracy hides this because the classes are imbalanced.
Precision is undefined or meaningless when the model never predicts positive; recall shows the failure.
More data would not change the fact that the model finds no positives.

questions.question: What must be true of base models for an ensemble to be effective?
questions.explanation: Diversity can come from different algorithms, different training data (bagging) or different feature sets.
questions.concept: Errors that differ can cancel; errors that match cannot.
options: They must all be identical copies of the best model
They must each be more accurate than any single strong model
They must all use the same features and data
They must be diverse, making uncorrelated errors
whyWrong: Identical models make the same mistakes, so combining them adds nothing.
Ensembles combine weak learners into a strong one.
Different data or features are ways to create diversity.

questions.question: Match each ensemble type to how it combines models.
questions.explanation: These four archetypes differ in whether models are trained in parallel or in sequence and how their outputs are combined.
questions.concept: Parallel diversity, sequential correction, or learned combination.

pairs.right: Combines different models trained on the same data
Trains learners in parallel on random bootstrap samples
Trains learners in sequence, each correcting the previous errors
A meta-model learns how to combine base models' predictions

questions.question: If all the base models in an ensemble make the same mistakes, combining them will cancel those mistakes out.
questions.explanation: Errors cancel only when models make uncorrelated errors. Models that err together keep the same errors after voting.
questions.concept: Diversity is what lets an ensemble beat its members.

questions.question: Three models give these probabilities for class 1 on one example: 0.90, 0.40 and 0.40. Using a 0.5 threshold for each model, what do hard voting and soft voting predict?
questions.explanation: Hard voting counts labels: one vote for class 1, two for class 0. Soft voting averages probabilities: (0.9 + 0.4 + 0.4) / 3 ≈ 0.57, so class 1.
questions.concept: Soft voting lets confident predictions carry more weight.
options: Hard voting: class 0; soft voting: class 1
Hard voting: class 1; soft voting: class 0
Both predict class 0
Both predict class 1
whyWrong: Only one model votes for class 1, so hard voting gives class 0.
The average probability is about 0.57, above 0.5, so soft voting gives class 1.
Two of three models vote class 0, so hard voting gives class 0.

questions.question: A team combines three logistic regression models, each trained on the same full dataset with the same features and settings, into a voting ensemble. The ensemble performs exactly like a single model. What is the best explanation and fix?
questions.explanation: Ensembles rely on diversity. Identical models trained the same way produce correlated errors, so combining them changes nothing.
questions.concept: No diversity, no ensemble benefit.
options: Voting ensembles never work with logistic regression; switch to a single decision tree
Add more identical logistic regression models until accuracy improves
Use hard voting instead of soft voting
The models lack diversity; vary the algorithms, bootstrap samples or features
whyWrong: Any algorithm can be part of an ensemble; the problem is identical training.
More identical copies still make the same errors.
The voting method cannot help when every model gives the same prediction.

questions.question: In bagging, what does 'bootstrap' mean?
questions.explanation: Bootstrap aggregating trains independent models on random samples drawn with replacement, then aggregates them by majority vote.
questions.concept: Bootstrap = sample with replacement.
options: Sampling the training data with replacement
Sampling the training data without replacement
Training each model on the errors of the previous one
Selecting only the most important features
whyWrong: Bootstrapping samples with replacement, so some rows repeat and others are left out.
That describes boosting.
Random feature subsets are a random-forest addition, not the bootstrap itself.

questions.question: Bagging mainly reduces variance and has little effect on bias.
questions.explanation: Bagging stabilises high-variance models such as deep trees. Because it does not reduce bias much, it needs complex base learners.
questions.concept: Bagging tames variance.

questions.question: Roughly what fraction of training samples is left out of each bootstrap sample and can be used for out-of-bag evaluation?
questions.explanation: About 37% of samples are out-of-bag for each tree, giving a built-in validation set (oob_score=True in scikit-learn).
questions.concept: OOB samples act as free validation data.
options: About 10%
About 50%
About 37%
0%, because every sample is always included
whyWrong: Bootstrap sampling leaves out far more than 10%.
The expected fraction left out is about 37%, not half.
Sampling with replacement always leaves some samples out.

questions.question: Why does a random forest consider only a random subset of features at each split?
questions.explanation: Random forests combine bagging (row sampling) with random feature sub-sampling at each split, usually about sqrt(number of features).
questions.concept: Double randomness makes trees different from one another.
options: To make each individual tree more accurate than a fully grown tree
To decorrelate the trees so no single feature dominates, reducing variance
To reduce bias, which bagging cannot do
Because trees cannot use more than the square root of the features
whyWrong: Individual trees may be slightly weaker; the forest gains from diversity.
Feature randomness mainly reduces correlation and variance.
Trees can use all features; the restriction is deliberate.

questions.question: A single deep decision tree reaches 100% training accuracy but 72% test accuracy, and its predictions change a lot when a few training rows change. The dataset is small, so the team does not want to set aside a separate validation set. Which approach best fits the lecture?
questions.explanation: The symptoms (perfect training fit, unstable predictions) are high variance. Bagging and random forests stabilise high-variance trees, and OOB samples provide validation without a separate split.
questions.concept: Diagnose bias or variance first; bagging targets variance.
questions.source: Lec 4.1, slide 44, Lec 4.1, slide 45, Lec 4.1, slide 47
options: A random forest, using its out-of-bag score as built-in validation
AdaBoost with depth-1 stumps, because boosting mainly reduces variance
A single, even deeper decision tree to fit the data more closely
KNN with K = 1, because it needs no training phase at all
whyWrong: Boosting mainly reduces bias. The problem here is high variance.
A deeper tree increases variance further.
K = 1 is itself a high-variance model.

questions.question: Which weak learner does AdaBoost usually use?
questions.explanation: AdaBoost trains a model, increases the weight of misclassified points, and trains the next model on the reweighted data.
questions.concept: Boosting combines many weak rules into a strong one.
options: Fully grown decision trees
K-nearest neighbours with K = 1
Decision stumps (trees of depth 1)
Logistic regression meta-models
whyWrong: AdaBoost relies on weak learners; full trees are strong, high-variance learners.
KNN is not the standard AdaBoost learner.
Meta-models belong to stacking.

questions.question: In gradient boosting, each new tree is trained to predict the original target y directly.
questions.explanation: Each new tree is fitted to the residuals (the negative gradient of the loss), that is, to how much the previous trees got wrong.
questions.concept: Each new tree predicts the current errors.

questions.question: Match each boosting library to its key innovation.
questions.explanation: XGBoost adds L1/L2 regularisation, sparse-data handling and parallel tree construction. LightGBM grows leaf-wise. CatBoost uses ordered boosting.
questions.concept: Each library improves boosting in a different direction.

pairs.right: Regularised boosting
Leaf-wise tree growth for large-scale data
Ordered boosting, strong with categorical data

questions.question: What is the trade-off when the learning rate of a boosting model is lowered?
questions.explanation: The learning rate scales each tree's contribution. A lower rate needs more estimators but gives better generalisation, as in the lecture's example of 1,000 trees at 0.01.
questions.concept: Small steps, more trees, better generalisation.
options: Fewer trees are needed, and training becomes faster
More trees are needed, but the model usually generalises better
The model can no longer overfit, however many trees are added
Nothing changes, because the learning rate only affects random forests
whyWrong: A lower learning rate needs more trees, not fewer.
Boosting can still overfit with too many trees.
The learning rate is a key boosting hyperparameter.

questions.question: A factory uses AdaBoost to flag defective parts. Five training parts start with equal weights of 0.2. The first stump misclassifies parts 2 and 4. Using the lecture's rule of doubling the weight of each misclassified part and then normalising so the weights sum to 1, what are the new weights?
questions.explanation: After doubling: [0.2, 0.4, 0.2, 0.4, 0.2], which sums to 1.4. Dividing by 1.4 gives about [0.143, 0.286, 0.143, 0.286, 0.143]. The next stump will focus on parts 2 and 4.
questions.concept: Boosting re-weights the data toward the hard cases.
questions.source: Lec 4.1, slide 50, Lec 4.1, slide 51, Lec 4.1, slide 52
options: About 0.143 for parts 1, 3 and 5, and about 0.286 for parts 2 and 4
0.2 for parts 1, 3 and 5, and 0.4 for parts 2 and 4
0.1 for parts 2 and 4, and 0.2 for the rest
0.2 for every part, because AdaBoost keeps weights equal
whyWrong: These weights sum to 1.4; they must be normalised to sum to 1.
Misclassified parts get more weight, not less.
AdaBoost increases the weight of misclassified samples so the next learner focuses on them.

questions.question: In stacking, what does the meta-model learn?
questions.explanation: Stacking trains base models (for example KNN, random forest and logistic regression), collects their predictions, and trains a meta-model on those predictions.
questions.concept: Stacking learns how to combine models instead of using a fixed vote.
options: Which base model to trust for each kind of input, from their predictions
How to predict from the original features while ignoring the base models
How to fit the residuals left by the previous tree in a sequence
How to sample the training data with replacement for each model
whyWrong: The meta-model is trained on the base models' predictions.
That describes gradient boosting.
That describes bagging.

questions.question: Boosting trains models sequentially, with each new model focusing on the samples its predecessors found hard.
questions.explanation: Unlike bagging, boosting is sequential, and each model attempts to correct the errors of the one before.
questions.concept: Bagging is parallel; boosting is sequential.

questions.question: Why is Gini impurity often preferred over entropy in CART decision trees?
questions.explanation: Gini = 1 - sum(p²) avoids a log calculation, so it is faster, and splits are usually similar to those chosen by entropy.
questions.concept: Gini and entropy rank splits similarly; Gini is cheaper.
options: It always produces much more accurate trees than entropy does
It can measure impurity for regression targets only
It is faster because it needs no logarithm, with very similar results
It reaches its maximum value of 1 for a pure node
whyWrong: The lecture says the results are usually very similar.
Gini is a classification criterion.
Gini is 0 for a pure node.

questions.question: Why does bagging work best with complex base learners such as deep decision trees?
questions.explanation: Averaging many high-variance, low-bias models cancels out their variance. Averaging many high-bias models would leave the bias in place.
questions.concept: Bagging fixes variance, so start from low-bias learners.
options: Because bagging mainly reduces bias, so it needs learners with high variance
Because simple learners cannot be trained on bootstrap samples
Bagging mainly reduces variance, not bias, so each base learner must already have low bias
Because deep trees make the ensemble sequential
whyWrong: Bagging reduces variance; it has little effect on bias.
Any learner can be trained on a bootstrap sample.
Bagging trains learners in parallel whatever their depth.

questions.question: Why is soft voting generally better than hard voting?
questions.explanation: Hard voting counts one vote per model. Soft voting averages probabilities, so a model that is 90% sure counts more than one that is 51% sure.
questions.concept: Soft voting keeps the confidence information that hard voting throws away.
options: It ignores the least accurate model in the ensemble
It only needs one model to produce probabilities
Confident probability estimates count for more
It always picks the class chosen by most models
whyWrong: Soft voting averages all models' probabilities; it ignores none.
Every model must provide probabilities for soft voting.
That is hard voting.

questions.question: Which of these is a regression task?
questions.explanation: Regression predicts a number on a continuous scale, such as a price, a temperature or a score.
questions.concept: If the answer is a number on a continuous scale, it is regression.
options: Deciding whether an email is spam
Predicting tomorrow's maximum temperature in °C
Predicting whether a student will pass or fail
Identifying which species a flower belongs to
whyWrong: Spam or not spam is a label, so this is classification.
Pass/fail is a label; the lecture says this is classification.
A species is a category, so this is classification.

questions.question: A residual is e = y - ŷ, so a positive residual means the model predicted too low.
questions.explanation: If the true value is larger than the prediction, y - ŷ is positive, which means the prediction was too low.
questions.concept: Residual = truth minus prediction.

questions.question: Regression vocabulary: match each word to what it refers to in a dataset or model.
questions.explanation: Features are also called predictors or independent variables, the target the response or dependent variable, and parameters weights or coefficients.
questions.concept: Shared vocabulary for every regression model.

pairs.right: One row of the dataset
An input column used to make the prediction
The true number we want to predict
A number inside the model that learning adjusts
The gap between truth and prediction

questions.question: The lecture summary says that in regression 'error is a distance, not a right-or-wrong count'. What does this mean?
questions.explanation: Because targets are continuous, an error has a size. Metrics such as MAE and RMSE summarise the size of those gaps.
questions.concept: Regression error has a size; classification error is a count.
options: Regression models are evaluated with accuracy, in the same way as classifiers
Errors in regression are always measured as physical distances in kilometres
A regression prediction counts as correct only if it matches exactly
Regression is judged by how far off predictions are, not by counting correct answers
whyWrong: Accuracy counts correct labels; regression uses MAE, MSE, RMSE and R².
'Distance' means the size of the gap between prediction and truth, not physical distance.
Exact matches are rare for continuous values; what matters is how close predictions are.

questions.question: A hospital wants three models. (a) Predict how many days a patient will stay. (b) Predict whether a patient will be readmitted within 30 days (yes or no). (c) Predict a disease-progression score between 25 and 346. Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: The output decides the task: numbers on a continuous scale for regression, labels for classification.
questions.concept: Look at the target, not the features.
options: (a) and (c) are regression tasks; (b) is classification
All three are regression, because they all use numeric patient features
Only (c) is regression, because length of stay is a count
(b) is regression, because readmission is coded as 0 and 1
whyWrong: The type of task is decided by the target. A yes/no target is classification.
Length of stay is a number on a numeric scale and is predicted as regression.
Coding a label as 0/1 does not make it continuous; it is still a category.

questions.question: In ŷ = β0 + β1x1 + ... + βpxp, what does the intercept β0 represent?
questions.explanation: The intercept sets the height of the line. With centred data, x = 0 is the average, so β0 is the prediction at average feature values.
questions.concept: Intercept = height; weights = slopes.
options: The change in prediction when x1 rises by one unit
The average residual
The number of features in the model
The prediction when every feature equals zero
whyWrong: That is the weight β1.
Residuals are errors; the intercept is a parameter.
β0 is a parameter value, not a count.

questions.question: In multiple linear regression, a coefficient βj shows the change in the prediction when xj rises by one unit while the other features are allowed to change freely.
questions.explanation: Each coefficient is the effect of its feature while every other feature is held constant.
questions.concept: Read each weight with all other features fixed.

questions.question: A linear regression with two features draws which shape?
questions.explanation: One feature draws a line, two draw a plane and many draw a hyperplane; the way you read each weight never changes.
questions.concept: More features add dimensions; interpretation stays the same.
options: A flat plane
A straight line
A curve that bends
A hyperplane in exactly two dimensions
whyWrong: One feature draws a line.
A linear model with only original features cannot bend.
Hyperplanes are the general term for many features; two features give a plane.

questions.question: A model predicts exam marks as ŷ = 20 + 3 × study_hours + 0.5 × attendance_percent. What is the prediction for a student with 4 study hours and 80% attendance?
questions.concept: Plug each feature into the equation and add the intercept.
whyWrong: This is 20 + 40, leaving out the study-hours term 3 × 4 = 12.
This uses the full attendance value 80 instead of 0.5 × 80 = 40.
This is 20 + 12, leaving out the attendance term entirely.

questions.question: A housing model is ŷ = 50,000 + 1,200 × area_m2 - 3,000 × age_years. An analyst writes: 'Each extra year of age causes the price to fall by $3,000, regardless of the size of the house.' Which correction is most accurate?
questions.explanation: Each weight is the change in the prediction per one-unit rise in its feature with other features held constant. The lecture stresses that such relationships are correlation, not proof of cause.
questions.concept: Coefficients are conditional associations.
questions.source: Lec 5.1, slide 5, Lec 5.1, slide 15, Lec 5.1, slide 16
options: Each extra year lowers the price by 3,000 percent, whatever the area of the house
With area fixed, each year goes with a $3,000 lower predicted price; this is association, not cause
The coefficient cannot be interpreted, because it is negative and prices cannot be
The intercept of $50,000 is the price of an average house, so the statement is fine
whyWrong: The coefficient is in the target's units (dollars), not a percentage.
A negative coefficient means the prediction falls as the feature rises; it is interpretable.
The intercept is the prediction when all features are zero, which here is not an average house.

questions.question: Why does the cost function J(β) square the residuals?
questions.explanation: Squaring makes every error positive and punishes one large miss far more than several small ones.
questions.concept: Squared error: no cancellation, heavy penalty for big misses.
options: So positive and negative errors cannot cancel, and large misses count more
So that the total cost always comes out as a negative number
So that every error counts equally, whatever its size
Because squaring removes outliers from the training data
whyWrong: Squared values are never negative.
Squaring makes large errors count much more.
Squaring makes outliers more influential, not removed.

questions.question: Minimising the sum of squared residuals instead of their average gives different β values.
questions.explanation: Dividing by n does not change where the minimum is, so the sum and the average give exactly the same β values.
questions.concept: Scaling the cost by a constant does not move its minimum.

questions.question: Match each piece of the learning process to its description.
questions.explanation: Both methods minimise the same cost. The normal equation β = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy is exact; gradient descent β ← β - η∇J(β) is iterative.
questions.concept: Exact in one step, or approximate in many small steps.

pairs.right: Solves for the best weights in one step; exact but heavy with many features
Walks downhill in small steps; scales to huge datasets
One number saying how wrong the model is
How far each gradient-descent update moves the weights

questions.question: When is gradient descent preferred over the normal equation?
questions.explanation: The normal equation is exact but heavy with many features. Gradient descent is slower per problem but scales to huge datasets.
questions.concept: Choose the solver by problem size.
options: When an exact solution is required rather than an approximate one
When the model has only one feature and very few rows of data
When there are very many features or rows, since the one-step solution gets heavy
When the cost function does not need to be minimised at all
whyWrong: The normal equation gives the exact solution.
That is the easiest case for the normal equation.
Both methods minimise the cost.
