questions.question: A student trains linear regression with gradient descent. Instead of falling steadily, the cost jumps up and down and grows larger with each iteration. Based on β ← β - η∇J(β), what is the most likely cause and fix?
questions.explanation: Gradient descent walks downhill in steps of size η. If the steps are too big, updates jump past the minimum and the cost can grow. This is an inference from the update rule; the slide describes η as the step size.
questions.concept: Small, steady steps downhill; oversized steps overshoot.
options: The relationship is non-linear, so gradient descent cannot be used
The cost should be changed to MAE so errors are not squared
The step size η is too large, so each update overshoots the minimum; reduce η
More features should be added so the cost has more directions to fall
whyWrong: Gradient descent works on this convex cost; growing cost points to the step size.
Changing the cost does not fix overshooting caused by large steps.
More features do not stop each step from overshooting.

questions.question: Match each L-I-N-E assumption to its meaning.
questions.explanation: L-I-N-E is the memory aid. Each assumption has a consequence if it fails.
questions.concept: Linearity, Independence, Normality, Equal variance.

pairs.right: Each feature moves the target in a straight line
One row tells you nothing about another row
Residuals are spread symmetrically around zero
The spread of residuals stays the same across the range

questions.question: The lecture says the linear-regression assumptions should be checked by plotting the residuals, not simply assumed.
questions.explanation: You test these conditions by plotting the residuals, never by assuming.
questions.concept: Assumptions are checked with residual plots.

questions.question: Multicollinearity makes the weights more stable and easier to interpret.
questions.explanation: When two features carry almost the same information, the weights become unstable and lose their meaning.
questions.concept: Near-duplicate features destabilise coefficients.

questions.question: A residual plot shows residuals spreading wider and wider as the predicted value increases, forming a funnel. Which assumption is violated?
questions.explanation: Fan-shaped residuals indicate heteroscedasticity: the model is accurate for some values and poor for others.
questions.concept: U-shape: non-linear. Funnel: unequal variance.
options: Linearity, shown by a U-shaped curve
Independence of rows
No assumption is violated; funnels are expected
Equal variance (the errors are heteroscedastic)
whyWrong: A U-shape signals non-linearity; a funnel signals unequal variance.
Independence is about rows being unrelated, not about the spread of residuals.
A funnel shows that accuracy varies across the range.

questions.question: A shop models daily sales using two years of data. Sales on consecutive days are strongly related (a busy day is usually followed by another busy day). The rows are shuffled randomly into training and test sets, and the test R² looks impressive. Which assumption is at risk, and what is the consequence?
questions.explanation: When one row tells you something about another, the independence assumption fails, and the lecture notes the model then looks better than it is.
questions.concept: Related rows make evaluation optimistic.
options: Normality of errors: p-values cannot be trusted, but the R² is reliable
Linearity: the model underfits, and the residuals follow a curved pattern
No assumption is at risk, because shuffling makes rows independent
Independence: related rows land in both sets, so the model looks better than it is
whyWrong: The issue is that rows are related, which inflates performance estimates.
Nothing in the scenario indicates curved relationships.
Shuffling changes row order, not the relationship between neighbouring days.

questions.question: Which family of regression models can delete useless features automatically while fitting?
questions.explanation: Ridge and Lasso add a penalty on large weights. Lasso can drive weights exactly to zero, deleting features.
questions.concept: Lasso selects features while it fits.
options: Regularised models such as Lasso
Polynomial regression models
Plain linear regression
Kernel and neural models
whyWrong: Polynomial regression adds features; it does not remove them.
Ordinary least squares keeps every feature.
These learn complex shapes but do not perform this kind of feature deletion.

questions.question: Tree-based regression models split the data into regions and predict an average value within each region.
questions.explanation: Tree models handle curves and interactions with no equation at all, predicting the average of each region.
questions.concept: Regression trees predict region averages.

questions.question: Why can the coefficients of the scikit-learn diabetes model be compared directly as importance scores?
questions.explanation: Every feature is mean-centred and scaled, so coefficients share one scale and can be compared directly.
questions.concept: Coefficients are comparable only when features share a scale.
options: All ten features are already standardised to the same scale
Because the target has been converted to a 0/1 label
Because the dataset has no missing values
Because there are exactly 442 patients
whyWrong: The target is a continuous progression score from 25 to 346.
Missing values do not affect coefficient comparability.
Sample size does not make coefficients comparable; a shared scale does.

questions.question: Why does the lecture describe linear regression as 'the baseline every model must beat'?
questions.explanation: A simple, interpretable baseline shows how much extra value more complex models really add.
questions.concept: Complexity must earn its place against a simple baseline.
options: Complex models must clearly beat this fast, readable model
It is always the most accurate model available for tabular data
It is the only model that can be evaluated with RMSE and R²
It cannot overfit under any circumstances, whatever the features
whyWrong: The lecture says tree ensembles are usually the most accurate for table-shaped data.
Every regression model can be evaluated with RMSE.
Any model can overfit in some settings; the point is simplicity and readability.

questions.question: A team has 300 rows of tabular data with curved relationships and interactions between features. They want the most accurate model they can reasonably build and will compare it with a simple benchmark. Which plan best follows the lecture?
questions.explanation: The lecture calls linear regression the baseline and ensembles of trees usually the most accurate choice for table-shaped data, while neural models need far more data.
questions.concept: Baseline first, then the family that suits the data.
options: Fit linear regression as the baseline, then try a tree ensemble
Go straight to a large neural network, because it learns the most complex shapes
Use a degree-10 polynomial so every curve is captured
Use only linear regression, because it is the most readable
whyWrong: Neural models need far more data and tuning than 300 rows allow.
High-degree polynomials follow every wobble and overfit badly.
A straight-line model underfits curves and interactions; it serves as the baseline.

questions.question: Match each metric to its behaviour.
questions.explanation: MAE and RMSE are in the target's units, MSE is in squared units, and R² is unitless.
questions.concept: Report RMSE with R²: typical error size plus variance explained.

pairs.right: Treats every error equally; robust to outliers
Squares errors so outliers dominate; used as the training loss
Keeps MSE's outlier sensitivity but reads in the target's units
Share of the target's variance that the model explains

questions.question: R² can be negative when a model performs worse than simply predicting the mean.
questions.explanation: R² = 1 - SSR/SST. A value of 0 equals predicting the mean, and a negative value is worse than the mean.
questions.concept: R² compares the model with always predicting the mean.

questions.question: Which metric is expressed in the square of the target's units?
questions.explanation: Squaring the errors squares the units; RMSE takes the square root to return to the original units.
questions.concept: Squared errors, squared units.
options: MAE
MSE
RMSE
R²
whyWrong: MAE is in the same units as the target.
Taking the square root returns RMSE to the target's units.
R² is unitless.

questions.question: A model's errors on five test points are 2, -2, 4, -4 and 10. Which set of metric values is correct?
questions.explanation: MAE = (2 + 2 + 4 + 4 + 10) / 5 = 4.4. MSE = (4 + 4 + 16 + 16 + 100) / 5 = 28. RMSE = sqrt(28) ≈ 5.29. The single error of 10 contributes 100 of the 140 squared total.
questions.concept: Squaring lets one large error dominate.
questions.source: Lec 5.1, slide 18, Lec 5.1, slide 19, Lec 5.1, slide 20
options: MAE = 2.0, MSE = 28, RMSE ≈ 5.29
MAE = 4.4, MSE = 28, RMSE ≈ 5.29
MAE = 4.4, MSE ≈ 5.29, RMSE = 28
whyWrong: MAE uses absolute errors; the signed errors averaging to 2 is the mean error, not MAE.
140 is the sum of squared errors; MSE divides it by 5.
MSE and RMSE are swapped.

questions.question: A courier compares two delivery-time models. Model A: MAE 5 min, RMSE 6 min. Model B: MAE 4.5 min, RMSE 12 min. Occasional very late estimates cause serious customer complaints. Which model should be preferred, and why?
questions.explanation: MSE and RMSE square errors, so a few large misses raise RMSE sharply. A big gap between MAE and RMSE signals large errors.
questions.concept: Compare MAE with RMSE to detect large errors.
options: Model B, because it has the lower MAE of the two models
Neither can be compared, because MAE and RMSE are in different units
Model B, because a higher RMSE means more of the variance is explained
Model A: its RMSE is close to its MAE, so it makes few very large errors
whyWrong: MAE treats every error equally and hides the few large misses that the business cares about.
Both are in minutes, the target's units.
RMSE measures error size; variance explained is R².

questions.question: On an actual-versus-predicted plot, where would the points lie for a perfect model?
questions.explanation: When predictions equal actual values, every point satisfies predicted = actual, which is the diagonal. Deviations show systematic over- or under-prediction.
questions.concept: Distance from the diagonal is error.
options: On a horizontal line at the mean
Randomly scattered across the plot
On the 45-degree diagonal line
On a vertical line at zero
whyWrong: A horizontal line means the model predicts the same value for everyone.
Random scatter means the predictions are unrelated to the truth.
That has no meaning for actual vs predicted values.

questions.question: A U-shaped pattern in a residual plot suggests the relationship is non-linear.
questions.explanation: Residuals should be random around zero. A U-shape implies non-linearity; a funnel implies heteroscedasticity.
questions.concept: Patterns in residuals mean the model missed structure.

questions.question: High bias describes a model that is too complex and overfits.
questions.explanation: High bias means the model is too simple (underfitting). High variance means it is too complex (overfitting).
questions.concept: Bias: too simple. Variance: too complex.

questions.question: What is the goal of the bias-variance trade-off?
questions.explanation: Too simple a model misses patterns; too complex a model learns noise. The best complexity balances both.
questions.concept: Total error is lowest at the right complexity.
options: To make the model as complex as possible so training error reaches zero
To find the complexity that minimises total error
To remove variance entirely, whatever happens to bias
To choose the model with the highest bias, because it is most stable
whyWrong: Zero training error usually means overfitting.
Pushing variance to zero makes the model too simple and raises bias.
High bias means underfitting.

questions.question: Three polynomial models were fitted. X (degree 1): training RMSE 18, validation RMSE 19. Y (degree 12): training RMSE 3, validation RMSE 25. Z (degree 3): training RMSE 9, validation RMSE 10. Which diagnosis and choice are correct?
questions.explanation: Underfitting shows as high error on both sets; overfitting as low training error with much higher validation error. Z balances the two and has the lowest validation error.
questions.concept: Pick complexity by validation error, and read the gap to diagnose.
options: Y should be chosen, because it has the lowest training error
X has high variance and Y has high bias
X should be chosen, because its training and validation errors are closest
X has high bias, Y has high variance, and Z should be chosen
whyWrong: Y's large gap between training and validation error shows overfitting.
This reverses the definitions: X underfits (both errors high), Y overfits (large gap).
Close errors are good, but X's are both high, which means underfitting.

questions.question: In K-fold cross-validation, how often does each fold serve as the validation set?
questions.explanation: The data are split into K folds, and every row gets a turn as validation, which reduces the risk of a lucky or unlucky single split.
questions.concept: Every row gets a turn as validation.
options: Never; it is only used for training
K times
Only in the final fold
Exactly once
whyWrong: Every fold takes one turn as validation.
Each fold is validation once and training K - 1 times.
Every fold is used for validation, not just the last.

questions.question: K-fold cross-validation fits the model about K times, so it costs roughly K times the compute of a single hold-out fit.
questions.explanation: Hold-out validation fits once and is cheap; K-fold fits K models and averages their scores.
questions.concept: Stability costs compute.

questions.question: Tuning hyperparameters on the test set is acceptable as long as the test set is only checked a few times.
questions.explanation: Hyperparameters are tuned on validation folds only. The test set is touched once, at the very end, or the reported error is optimistic.
questions.concept: The test set is for one final check.

questions.question: Why does the lecture prefer K-fold cross-validation for the 442-patient diabetes dataset?
questions.explanation: Small datasets make hold-out estimates high-variance. K-fold averages K scores and also gives a standard deviation.
questions.concept: Small data favours K-fold.
options: Because K-fold needs fewer model fits than a single hold-out validation
A single hold-out score on so few rows depends on which rows it gets
Because hold-out validation cannot be used for regression problems
Because K-fold removes the need for a final, untouched test set
whyWrong: K-fold needs about K fits.
Hold-out works for regression; it is just less stable on small data.
The test set is still touched once at the end.

questions.question: A team tries 50 values of Ridge's alpha, picks the one with the best test-set R² (0.61), and reports 0.61 as the model's expected performance on new patients. What is the best critique?
questions.explanation: The lecture's non-negotiable rule: tune hyperparameters on validation folds only, and touch the test set once at the very end.
questions.concept: Tune on validation, report on an untouched test set.
options: The approach is correct, because the best test score is the most honest estimate
Alpha was tuned on the test set, so 0.61 is optimistic; tune with CV and test once at the end
The only problem is that 50 values is too few, so more alphas should be tried
R² should be replaced by MAE, which removes the bias from the reported score
whyWrong: Selecting the best of 50 test scores uses the test set for tuning, which biases the estimate upward.
The number of values is not the issue; where they were evaluated is.
Changing the metric does not fix tuning on the test set.

questions.question: Why is polynomial regression still called a linear model?
questions.explanation: Adding x², x³ or products creates new columns, but the prediction is still a weighted sum of columns, so the fitting does not change.
questions.concept: Linear in β, not necessarily in x.
options: Because the fitted curve is always a straight line, whatever the degree
It is still linear in its coefficients β; only new columns are added
Because polynomial terms are removed again before fitting
Because it can only be used with one input feature at a time
whyWrong: Polynomial terms let the fitted curve bend.
The terms are kept; they are the new columns.
Polynomial features can be built from several features and their products.

questions.question: Match each item to its effect.
questions.explanation: The penalised loss is MSE + λ × penalty. λ controls how much large weights cost.
questions.concept: λ sets the strength; L1 selects, L2 shrinks.

pairs.right: Shrinks every coefficient towards zero, never exactly to zero
Can drive coefficients exactly to zero
Gives ordinary least squares
Flattens coefficients so the model drifts towards predicting the mean

questions.question: In scikit-learn, setting Ridge's alpha to 0 applies the strongest possible penalty.
questions.explanation: alpha is the penalty strength (λ). alpha = 0 means no penalty, which is ordinary least squares.
questions.concept: alpha = λ; zero means no regularisation.

questions.question: As the polynomial degree increases, what happens to bias and variance?
questions.explanation: Degree 1 has high bias and underfits curves; degree 10 follows every wobble and has high variance. Degree 2 to 3 is usually the sweet spot, chosen by cross-validation.
questions.concept: Degree sets the position on the bias-variance trade-off.
options: Bias increases and variance decreases
Both decrease
Both stay the same, because the model is still linear in β
Bias decreases and variance increases
whyWrong: Higher degree makes the model more flexible, lowering bias and raising variance.
Flexibility does not reduce both at once; that is the trade-off.
Being linear in β does not stop flexibility from growing.

questions.question: A team has 200 samples and 150 features, many of which are probably irrelevant. They want a model that keeps only a small number of features so clinicians can read it. Which approach fits best?
questions.explanation: Lasso's L1 penalty performs automatic feature selection while fitting. Alpha should be tuned on validation folds.
questions.concept: Need fewer features? Use L1.
options: Ridge, because it removes irrelevant features by setting them to zero
Lasso, with alpha chosen by cross-validation
Ordinary least squares with alpha = 0, to avoid any penalty
Polynomial features of degree 3, to capture more patterns
whyWrong: Ridge shrinks coefficients but never exactly to zero, so all 150 features remain.
No penalty means no selection, and 150 features on 200 samples risks large, unstable weights.
This adds many more features, the opposite of what is needed.

questions.question: What 'double randomness' makes the trees in a random forest regressor different from one another?
questions.explanation: Random data samples plus random feature subsets decorrelate the trees, which is why many trees beat one tree.
questions.concept: Decorrelated trees average out each other's errors.
options: A random sample of rows and a random subset of features
A random learning rate and a random tree depth
Fitting each tree to the residuals of the previous one
A different, randomly chosen target variable
whyWrong: Random forests do not randomise the learning rate; that is a boosting parameter.
That is boosting.
Every tree predicts the same target.

questions.question: In boosting, the trees are grown independently and in parallel, like in a random forest.
questions.explanation: Random forests grow trees independently. Boosting grows them one after another, each fitted to the errors left so far.
questions.concept: Forest: parallel. Boosting: sequential.

questions.question: Match each gradient-boosting setting to the reason it is used.
questions.explanation: Shrinkage is the main guard against overfitting; shallow trees keep boosting meaningful; subsampling adds randomness.
questions.concept: Small steps, weak learners, random subsets.

pairs.right: Shrinks each tree's contribution, so more trees are needed
Keeps each tree a weak learner
Fits each tree on a random part of the data (stochastic boosting)

questions.question: A random forest regressor fits the training data almost perfectly but performs poorly on test data. Which change is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Deep trees have high variance and capture noise. Limiting depth, or increasing min_samples_split, forces simpler, more general patterns.
questions.concept: Shallower trees generalise better.
options: Increase max_depth
Remove the test set and evaluate on training data
Decrease max_depth
Decrease min_samples_split
whyWrong: Deeper trees capture even more noise, increasing overfitting.
This hides the problem rather than fixing it.
Allowing splits on fewer samples lets trees grow more complex.

questions.question: A random forest on patient data gives these importances: BMI 0.35, S5 0.30, blood pressure 0.12, other serum measures smaller, and sex 0.01. A manager concludes: 'BMI causes disease progression, and sex can be dropped.' Which response is most accurate?
questions.explanation: Tree-based models rank BMI and S5 as most influential, and features with near-zero importance can often be dropped without losing accuracy. Neither statement establishes cause.
questions.concept: Importance describes the model, not the world.
options: The model relies most on BMI and S5 and may not need sex, but importance is not causation
Both conclusions are correct, because importance measures each feature's causal effect
Neither conclusion holds, because random forests cannot rank features at all
Sex must be kept, because low importance means the model has not learned it yet
whyWrong: Feature importance shows what the model uses; the lecture warns that associations are not proof of cause.
Random forests provide feature importances, as the lecture's code shows.
Near-zero importance suggests the feature adds little, so dropping it is reasonable after checking accuracy.

questions.question: Does boosting mainly reduce bias or variance, and why?
questions.explanation: Each tree is fitted to the residuals left behind, so the ensemble steadily reduces systematic error. Gradient boosting is gradient descent in function space.
questions.concept: Bagging tames variance; boosting attacks bias.
options: Variance, because trees are averaged in parallel
Neither, because boosting only speeds up training
Bias, because each new tree corrects the remaining errors
Variance, because each tree is fully grown
whyWrong: Parallel averaging describes bagging, which mainly reduces variance.
Boosting reduces error tree by tree; it is not a speed technique.
Boosting uses shallow, weak trees.

questions.question: Ensembles combine multiple weak learners to create a strong learner, reducing error by averaging out individual models' biases or variances.
questions.explanation: This is the 'wisdom of the crowd' idea behind random forests and boosting.
questions.concept: Many weak learners can make one strong learner.

questions.question: What split does the lecture describe as standard practice for a medium-sized dataset?
questions.explanation: An 80/20 split trains on one part and judges on the other, so the model is evaluated on unseen data.
questions.concept: Train on one part, judge on the other.
options: 50% training, 50% test
80% training, 20% test
100% training, evaluated on the same data
20% training, 80% test
whyWrong: This wastes a large share of data on testing.
Evaluating on training data does not measure generalisation.
This leaves too little data to fit the model.

questions.question: MAE is easier to explain, so why is MSE usually the loss used to train regression models?
questions.explanation: The lecture's metrics table describes MSE as smooth and differentiable, hence used as the training loss, while MAE is robust and easy to explain to clinicians.
questions.concept: Train with a loss that is easy to optimise; report metrics that are easy to read.
options: MSE is robust to outliers, unlike MAE
MSE is reported in the same units as the target
MSE is smooth and differentiable, which suits gradient descent
MSE always gives a higher R² than MAE
whyWrong: MSE is more sensitive to outliers, because errors are squared.
MSE is in squared units; RMSE returns to the target's units.
R² is a separate metric; the choice of loss does not guarantee a higher R².
